sections.title: What makes a motion simple harmonic

board_events.text: From periodic motion to oscillation to SHM
Periodic motion repeats after a fixed time; an oscillation is periodic motion that goes to and fro about a fixed point.
SHM is the cleanest oscillation: the restoring force grows in exact proportion to the displacement.
The minus sign is the soul of SHM: the force always points back toward the mean position.

board_events.text: At the mean the pull is zero, so speed is greatest; at the extremes the pull is largest, so the particle freezes and reverses.
Speed is maximum where the force is zero; speed is zero where the force is maximum.

segments.text: <curious>Remember the last time you sat on a jhula in the courtyard and someone gave you a gentle push? You sail forward, slow down, stop, and come right back. We are going to build this whole chapter out of that one feeling.

First, some vocabulary. A motion that repeats after a fixed interval of time is called periodic, like the hands of a wall clock or the Earth going round the Sun. When that repeating motion goes to and fro about a central point, a swing or a tuning fork, we call it an oscillation.

Simple harmonic motion is the purest oscillation of all. It happens whenever the force dragging the body back to the centre grows in exact proportion to how far it has strayed. Stray a little, get pulled a little; stray twice as far, get pulled twice as hard.
In symbols, the restoring force equals minus k times x. Here k is the stiffness and x is the displacement measured from the mean position.

That minus sign is the entire soul of S H M. It says the force points opposite to the displacement, always back toward home. When you are to the right, it pulls left; when you are to the left, it pushes right.

Picture it on a straight line. The particle is pulled toward the centre from either side, exactly like a rubber band tied to your finger, which tugs harder the more you stretch it and always toward the finger, never away.
At the mean position the tug is zero, so the particle races through fastest right there. At the turning points the tug is largest, so it momentarily freezes and reverses direction.
So hold on to this one sentence. Speed is maximum where the force is zero, and speed is zero where the force is maximum. Almost every S H M question you will meet is just a variation of this picture.
याद है वो jhula वाला moment, जब कोई gentle push देता है और आप आगे जाते हो, फिर slow होकर रुकते हो और वापस आ जाते हो? पूरा chapter इसी feeling से बनेगा.

पहले थोड़ी vocabulary. जो motion किसी fixed time के बाद repeat होती है वो periodic कहलाती है, जैसे wall clock की सुई या Earth का Sun के around घूमना. और जब यही repeating motion किसी central point के around to and fro होती है, तो उसे oscillation कहते हैं.

<curious>Simple harmonic motion इन सब में सबसे pure oscillation है. ये तब होती है जब body को centre की तरफ खींचने वाली restoring force displacement के exactly proportional हो. थोड़ा हटो तो थोड़ा खिंचाव, दुगुना हटो तो दुगुना खिंचाव.
Symbols में restoring force बराबर है minus k times x. यहाँ k है stiffness और x है mean position से measure किया गया displacement.
यही minus sign S H M की असली आत्मा है. ये बताता है कि force हमेशा displacement के opposite होती है, यानी वापस home की तरफ. right में हो तो left खींचती है, left में हो तो right धकेलती है.
इसे एक line पर सोचो. particle दोनों तरफ से centre की तरफ खिंचती है, बिलकुल finger पर बंधे rubber band की तरह, जो जितना stretch करो उतना ज़्यादा खींचे, और हमेशा finger की तरफ.
Mean position पर tug zero है, इसलिए particle वहीं सबसे fast दौड़ती है. turning points पर tug सबसे बड़ी है, इसलिए वो पल भर के लिए freeze होकर reverse कर जाती है.
तो एक line पक्की याद रखो: जहाँ force zero वहाँ speed maximum, और जहाँ force maximum वहाँ speed zero. लगभग हर S H M question इसी picture का variation है.

board_events.text: Any motion with acceleration proportional to $x$ and opposite in sign is SHM, whatever dressing the problem wears.
SHM is an idealisation, and exams love to test where it breaks.
The restoring force must be exactly linear (the Hooke region); a pendulum is SHM only for small angles where $\sin\theta \approx \theta$.
Ideal SHM assumes no damping and a single frequency; a sum of two different frequencies is periodic but not SHM.

segments.text: Now let us stamp S H M with its official identity card. Because force equals mass times acceleration, the force law we just wrote turns straight into a statement about acceleration.
Take F equals minus k x, and replace F by m times a. Dividing across by the mass, the acceleration becomes minus k over m, times x.

<excited>And there it is: acceleration equals minus omega squared times x, where omega squared is defined as k over m. This is the I D card of S H M. Two features matter, the proportionality to displacement and the minus sign.

Plot acceleration against displacement and you get a straight line through the origin with a negative slope. The steepness of that line is omega squared. At plus A the acceleration is most negative; at minus A it is most positive.
So the rule is simple. Any motion whose acceleration is proportional to displacement and points opposite to it is simple harmonic, no matter what disguise the question puts on.
But remember, S H M is an idealisation, and the examiner loves the places where the idealisation cracks.

The restoring force has to be exactly linear in displacement, which a real spring obeys only inside its elastic limit. A simple pendulum is simple harmonic only for small swings, where the sine of theta is approximately theta.
And ideal S H M assumes no damping and a single frequency. Add friction and the amplitude decays; add a second frequency and the motion is periodic but no longer simple harmonic.
अब S H M को उसका official identity card देते हैं. चूँकि force बराबर होता है mass times acceleration, इसलिए हमारा force law सीधे acceleration की एक statement बन जाता है.
F बराबर minus k x लो, और F की जगह रखो m times a. दोनों तरफ mass से divide करो तो acceleration बन जाता है minus k over m, times x.

<excited>और यही तो है: acceleration बराबर minus omega squared times x, जहाँ omega squared define होता है k over m. यही S H M का I D card है. दो चीज़ें matter करती हैं, displacement के साथ proportionality और वो minus sign.

Acceleration को displacement के against plot करो तो origin से गुज़रती एक straight line मिलती है, negative slope के साथ. उस line की steepness omega squared है. plus A पर acceleration सबसे negative, minus A पर सबसे positive.
तो rule simple है. जिस motion का acceleration displacement के proportional हो और उसके opposite point करे, वो simple harmonic है, चाहे question कोई भी disguise पहन ले.
पर याद रखो, S H M एक idealisation है, और examiner को वो जगहें बहुत पसंद हैं जहाँ ये idealisation टूटती है.

restoring force displacement में exactly linear होनी चाहिए, जो real spring सिर्फ़ अपनी elastic limit के अंदर मानता है. simple pendulum सिर्फ़ small swings पर simple harmonic है, जहाँ sine theta लगभग theta होता है.
और ideal S H M मानता है no damping और single frequency. friction डालो तो amplitude decay होती है; दूसरी frequency डालो तो motion periodic तो रहती है पर simple harmonic नहीं रहती.

sections.title: Key formulas and definitions

board_events.text: The complete kinematics toolkit

board_events.caption: Velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle; acceleration is anti-phase

board_events.text: Two shortcuts: $\omega = a_{\max}/v_{\max}$ and $A = v_{\max}^2/a_{\max}$.

segments.text: Let us lay out the complete toolkit for the kinematics of S H M. Everything on this board flows from a single sine.

Displacement is A sine of omega t plus phi. A is the amplitude, omega the angular frequency, and phi the starting phase. Using cosine instead is equally valid; it just starts the motion a quarter cycle earlier.

Differentiate once and velocity is A omega cosine of the same phase. Eliminate time and it becomes plus or minus omega, times the square root of A squared minus x squared, which is the form you will use most.
Differentiate again and acceleration is minus A omega squared sine, which is simply minus omega squared times x. The kinematics closes back on the I D card.
The bridges between omega, the period, and the frequency: omega equals two pi over T, and also two pi times f. Keep these ready because questions switch between them freely.

The two headline maxima: speed is greatest at the mean position, equal to A omega. Acceleration is greatest at the extremes, equal to A omega squared. Fastest in the middle, hardest-pulled at the ends.
The picture ties it together. Displacement is a sine, velocity a cosine that leads it by a quarter cycle, and acceleration a negative sine, exactly opposite to displacement.
<whisper>And two shortcuts worth gold in the exam hall: omega equals a-max divided by v-max, and A equals v-max squared divided by a-max. They crack objective questions in seconds.
चलो S H M की kinematics का पूरा toolkit board पर रख देते हैं. यहाँ सब कुछ एक ही sine से निकलता है.
Displacement है A sine omega t plus phi. A है amplitude, omega है angular frequency, और phi है starting phase. cosine use करना भी उतना ही सही है; बस motion एक quarter cycle पहले शुरू होती है.

एक बार differentiate करो तो velocity बनती है A omega cosine, उसी phase की. time हटाओ तो ये बन जाती है plus या minus omega, times square root of A squared minus x squared, जो form आप सबसे ज़्यादा use करोगे.
फिर से differentiate करो तो acceleration बनती है minus A omega squared sine, यानी simply minus omega squared times x. kinematics वापस उसी I D card पर बंद हो जाती है.
omega, period और frequency के बीच के bridges: omega बराबर two pi over T, और two pi times f भी. इन्हें ready रखो क्योंकि questions इनके बीच freely switch करते हैं.
<whisper>दो headline maxima: speed mean position पर सबसे ज़्यादा, बराबर A omega. acceleration extremes पर सबसे ज़्यादा, बराबर A omega squared. बीच में सबसे fast, किनारों पर सबसे ज़्यादा खिंचाव.
Picture सब जोड़ देती है. displacement एक sine, velocity एक cosine जो उससे एक quarter cycle आगे रहती है, और acceleration एक negative sine, displacement के बिलकुल opposite.
और दो shortcuts जो exam hall में सोने जैसे हैं: omega बराबर a-max divided by v-max, और A बराबर v-max squared divided by a-max. ये objective questions seconds में crack कर देते हैं.

sections.title: Derivation: velocity and acceleration from x(t)

board_events.text: Differentiating the displacement equation
Let the particle execute SHM with $A$ and $\phi$ constant.

board_events.caption: Velocity carries a cosine, so it peaks exactly where displacement is zero

board_events.text: The maths hands back $a = -\omega^2 x$, the very property we started from.
Physical reading: fastest at the mean, momentarily at rest at the extremes.

segments.text: Here is the first board derivation, the one C B S E asks for again and again. We start from the displacement of a particle in S H M and simply differentiate.
Let the particle move as A sine of omega t plus phi. The amplitude A and the phase constant phi are fixed numbers; only time changes.
Write down the starting equation clearly, because a clean start is half the derivation. Displacement equals A sine of omega t plus phi.

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, so differentiate once. The derivative of sine is cosine, and the chain rule brings out a factor of omega. Velocity becomes A omega cosine of omega t plus phi.

Read the physics off the picture. Displacement carries a sine, velocity carries a cosine, and cosine peaks exactly where sine is zero. So the particle moves fastest at the mean position and is momentarily at rest at the extremes.

Differentiate once more for acceleration. The derivative of cosine is minus sine, another omega drops out, and we get minus A omega squared sine. But A sine of that phase is just x, so acceleration equals minus omega squared times x.
<chuckle>Notice what happened. The maths handed us back the exact defining property we began with, acceleration equals minus omega squared x. That is a lovely consistency check.
And the physical picture is the swing all over again: quickest through the middle, frozen for an instant at the two ends before it turns.
ये रही पहली board derivation, वही जो C B S E बार बार पूछता है. हम S H M में particle के displacement से शुरू करते हैं और simply differentiate करते हैं.
मान लो particle चलती है A sine of omega t plus phi की तरह. amplitude A और phase constant phi fixed numbers हैं; सिर्फ़ time change होता है.
starting equation साफ़ लिखो, क्योंकि clean start आधी derivation होती है. displacement बराबर A sine of omega t plus phi.

Velocity displacement के change की rate है, तो एक बार differentiate करो. sine का derivative cosine होता है, और chain rule एक omega बाहर निकालता है. velocity बन जाती है A omega cosine of omega t plus phi.

अब physics picture से पढ़ो. displacement में sine, velocity में cosine, और cosine वहीं peak करता है जहाँ sine zero होता है. इसलिए particle mean position पर सबसे fast और extremes पर पल भर के लिए rest पर होती है.

<chuckle>एक बार और differentiate करो acceleration के लिए. cosine का derivative minus sine, एक और omega निकलता है, और मिलता है minus A omega squared sine. पर उस phase का A sine तो x ही है, तो acceleration बराबर minus omega squared times x.
देखो क्या हुआ. maths ने वही defining property वापस दे दी जिससे हमने शुरू किया था, acceleration बराबर minus omega squared x. ये एक बढ़िया consistency check है.
और physical picture फिर वही swing है: बीच से सबसे तेज़, और दोनों किनारों पर पल भर के लिए frozen, फिर मुड़ जाती है.

board_events.text: At $x=0$ this gives $v=\omega A$, the maximum; at $x=\pm A$ it gives $v=0$.
The plus-minus records two passes through each point: once forward, once back.

segments.text: Now the second derivation, and it is the workhorse of the whole chapter. We want velocity written in terms of position, with time completely eliminated, because problems almost always hand you where the particle is, not when.

Start from the two equations we already have. Divide the displacement equation by A, and divide the velocity equation by A omega. On the left we have x over A and v over A omega; on the right, a sine and a cosine of the same angle.
That is the setup, and it is deliberately arranged so the next step is a single identity.

Now use the identity sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. Squaring both fractions and adding, we get x squared over A squared, plus v squared over A squared omega squared, equal to one. The time has vanished.

Multiply through by A squared omega squared and rearrange. Velocity squared equals omega squared times the quantity A squared minus x squared. Take the root, and velocity equals plus or minus omega, root A squared minus x squared.
The picture makes it vivid. Plotted as v against x, this is an ellipse. Its width is set by the amplitude and its height by omega times the amplitude.

<curious>Read the two landmarks off the ellipse. At x equals zero, velocity is omega A, the maximum, right at the top and bottom of the ellipse. At x equal to plus or minus A, velocity is zero, where the ellipse touches the axis.
And the plus-or-minus is not clutter; it simply records that the particle passes each position twice, once moving forward and once moving back.
अब दूसरी derivation, और यही पूरे chapter की workhorse है. हमें velocity को position के terms में लिखना है, time पूरी तरह हटाकर, क्योंकि problems अक्सर बताते हैं particle कहाँ है, कब नहीं.

उन्हीं दो equations से शुरू करो जो हमारे पास हैं. displacement equation को A से divide करो, और velocity equation को A omega से. left पर मिलता है x over A और v over A omega; right पर एक ही angle के sine और cosine.
यही setup है, और इसे जानबूझकर ऐसे रखा गया है ताकि अगला step एक single identity बन जाए.

<curious>अब identity use करो, sine squared plus cosine squared बराबर one. दोनों fractions को square करके जोड़ो तो मिलता है x squared over A squared, plus v squared over A squared omega squared, बराबर one. time गायब हो गया.

पूरे को A squared omega squared से multiply करो और rearrange करो. velocity squared बराबर omega squared times A squared minus x squared. root लो, तो velocity बराबर plus या minus omega, root A squared minus x squared.
Picture इसे जीवंत कर देती है. v को x के against plot करो तो ये एक ellipse है. इसकी width amplitude से और height omega times amplitude से तय होती है.
ellipse से दो landmarks पढ़ो. x बराबर zero पर velocity omega A है, maximum, ellipse के top और bottom पर. x बराबर plus या minus A पर velocity zero, जहाँ ellipse axis को छूती है.
और वो plus-या-minus बेकार नहीं है; ये बस बताता है कि particle हर position से दो बार गुज़रती है, एक बार आगे जाते हुए और एक बार वापस आते हुए.

board_events.text: A mass $m$ feels a linear restoring force $F=-kx$; Newton's second law gives $ma=-kx$.
A stiffer spring pulls harder and oscillates faster; a heavier mass is more sluggish and slower.
The recipe: write the net force, show it equals minus (constant) times $x$, read $\omega^2$ off that constant.
This one recipe finds the period of every SHM system in the chapter.

segments.text: The third derivation is short but it is the master key. It tells you how to read the angular frequency directly from the force, and this single move unlocks every system in the chapter.
Picture the simplest case, a block on a spring against a wall. Displace it by x and the spring pulls back with a force minus k x, always toward the equilibrium mark.
Now bring in Newton. A mass m under this force obeys m times a equals minus k x. That is just the second law with the restoring force on the right.
Divide both sides by the mass. Acceleration equals minus k over m, times x. Notice the shape: acceleration is minus a constant, times displacement.

Compare that with the I D card, acceleration equals minus omega squared x. The constant sitting in front must be omega squared, so omega is the square root of k over m, and the period is two pi root m over k.
The physics is intuitive. A stiffer spring, a larger k, pulls harder and oscillates faster. A heavier mass, a larger m, is more sluggish and oscillates slower.
<excited>And here is the recipe to carry through the whole chapter. Write the net restoring force, force it into the shape minus constant times x, and simply read omega squared off that constant.
Pendulum, floating block, liquid in a tube, a body dropped through the Earth, every one of them yields to this same three-line move. Learn it once, use it everywhere.
तीसरी derivation छोटी है पर यही master key है. ये बताती है कि angular frequency सीधे force से कैसे पढ़ें, और यही एक move पूरे chapter का हर system खोल देता है.
सबसे simple case सोचो, wall के सामने spring पर एक block. उसे x से displace करो तो spring minus k x force से वापस खींचती है, हमेशा equilibrium mark की तरफ.

दोनों तरफ mass से divide करो. acceleration बराबर minus k over m, times x. shape देखो: acceleration है minus एक constant, times displacement.
<excited>इसे I D card से compare करो, acceleration बराबर minus omega squared x. आगे बैठा constant ही omega squared होना चाहिए, तो omega है square root of k over m, और period है two pi root m over k.
Physics intuitive है. stiffer spring, बड़ा k, ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींचती है और faster oscillate करती है. heavier mass, बड़ा m, ज़्यादा sluggish है और slower oscillate करती है.
और यही रही recipe जो पूरे chapter में काम आएगी. net restoring force लिखो, उसे minus constant times x के shape में लाओ, और उस constant से omega squared सीधे पढ़ लो.
Pendulum, floating block, tube में liquid, Earth में से गिरता body, हर एक इसी तीन-line move के आगे झुक जाता है. एक बार सीखो, हर जगह use करो.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): read off every quantity

board_events.text: Given a displacement equation, find all constants

board_events.caption: Amplitude is the height; period is the repeat length

board_events.text: Compare with $x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$: amplitude 0.05 m, angular frequency 20 pi, phase 0.

segments.text: Time for our first clean worked example, at C B S E board level. The whole art here is careful comparison, so let us do it slowly.
The particle is given by x equals zero point zero five, sine of twenty pi t, in S I units. Everything we need is hidden inside this one line.
Before touching numbers, picture what the equation says. The height of the wave is the amplitude; the horizontal distance for one full repeat is the period. The graph is our map.
Now compare term by term with the standard form, x equals A sine omega t plus phi. The amplitude A is zero point zero five metres, the angular frequency omega is twenty pi, and the phase phi is zero.
The period is two pi over omega, which is two pi over twenty pi, giving zero point one seconds. The frequency is one over the period, so ten hertz.
Maximum speed is A times omega, zero point zero five times twenty pi, which comes out as pi, about three point one four metres per second.
Maximum acceleration is A times omega squared, zero point zero five times twenty pi squared, which is twenty pi squared, about one hundred ninety seven point four metres per second squared.
<chuckle>Notice the clean discipline that scores full marks: identify the constants by comparison, substitute them in, and always attach the units. No shortcuts, no dropped units.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): the ratio shortcut

board_events.text: Max speed and max acceleration given, in thirty seconds
Given: maximum speed 8 pi cm/s and maximum acceleration 16 pi squared cm/s².
The trap: do not solve two simultaneous equations for $A$ and $\omega$.
Dividing $a_{\max}$ by $v_{\max}$ isolates $\omega$ instantly; that is the whole game.
This ratio is the single most reused trick in NEET oscillation questions.

segments.text: This one is a classic N E E T speed trap, and it is all about refusing to do the obvious slow thing.

The data: the particle has a maximum speed of eight pi centimetres per second and a maximum acceleration of sixteen pi squared centimetres per second squared. Find the amplitude and the period, in under thirty seconds.
Here is the trap that eats time. A student instinctively writes v-max equals A omega and a-max equals A omega squared, then tries to solve two messy equations together. Do not walk into that.
Instead, just divide. a-max divided by v-max is sixteen pi squared over eight pi, and almost everything cancels, leaving two pi. That is omega, in one clean step, in radians per second.
Once omega is known the period drops out. The period is two pi over omega, which is two pi over two pi, exactly one second.
And the amplitude is v-max over omega, eight pi over two pi, which is four centimetres. Two divisions, and we are done.
See why it works: dividing a-max by v-max cancels the amplitude and leaves omega alone. That single idea is the whole game.
<whisper>Lock it in. The ratio a-max over v-max giving omega is the single most reused trick in N E E T oscillation questions. If you see both maxima, divide first and think later.
ये एक classic N E E T speed trap है, और पूरा खेल obvious slow तरीका करने से मना करने का है.
data: particle की maximum speed eight pi centimetres per second और maximum acceleration sixteen pi squared centimetres per second squared. amplitude और period निकालो, thirty seconds के अंदर.

इसके बजाय, बस divide करो. a-max divided by v-max है sixteen pi squared over eight pi, और लगभग सब कुछ cancel होकर बचता है two pi. यही omega है, एक clean step में, radians per second में.

और amplitude है v-max over omega, eight pi over two pi, यानी four centimetres. दो divisions, और काम खत्म.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main favourite that links the position equation to the velocity-position relation. Whenever a problem gives you two speeds at two positions, this is the route.
Picture the two data points sitting on the velocity-position curve. Each pairs a position with a speed, and the curve passes through both. Our job is to pin down the amplitude and the period.
The data: the speed is sixteen centimetres per second when the particle is three centimetres from the mean, and twelve centimetres per second when it is four centimetres from the mean.

Use velocity equals omega root A squared minus x squared, and square it to kill the root. At three centimetres, sixteen squared, which is two hundred fifty six, equals omega squared times the quantity A squared minus nine.
At four centimetres, twelve squared, which is one hundred forty four, equals omega squared times the quantity A squared minus sixteen.

Now the key move. Subtract the second equation from the first. The A squared terms cancel, and two hundred fifty six minus one hundred forty four, which is one hundred twelve, equals seven omega squared. So omega squared is sixteen, and omega is four radians per second.

<excited>Put omega back into the first equation. Two hundred fifty six equals sixteen times A squared minus nine, so A squared minus nine is sixteen, giving amplitude five centimetres. The period is two pi over four, that is pi over two seconds.
The lesson to carry away: square the velocity-position relation at each point and subtract, and omega falls out in a single line. This is the standard route for every two-speeds problem.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): the one-third result

board_events.text: Fraction of a period with the displacement small
Prove the fraction of one period with the magnitude of $x$ less than $A/2$ is exactly one third.

board_events.caption: Time is proportional to swept angle on the reference circle

board_events.text: Take $x=A\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ sweeping 0 to $2\pi$; the condition becomes the magnitude of $\sin\theta$ under one half.
Equal angles take equal times, so reason about time on the phase circle, not a formula.
Fastest near the mean, so the particle lingers less per centimetre there.

segments.text: Let us finish with a J E E Advanced problem that rewards thinking over plugging. We must prove that the fraction of one full period during which the displacement stays smaller in magnitude than half the amplitude is exactly one third.
State the claim plainly first. Out of the whole to-and-fro, we want the slice of time the particle spends inside the central band, closer to the middle than half the amplitude on either side.

The clean tool is the reference circle, shown here. A steadily circulating radius casts a shadow that performs the S H M, and crucially, time is proportional to the angle swept, because equal angles take equal times.

So let x be A sine theta, with theta sweeping from zero to two pi across one period. The condition, magnitude of x under half the amplitude, then becomes simply the magnitude of sine theta under one half.

On the circle that holds in three windows, clustered around the mean-position crossings where sine is zero: theta from zero to pi over six, from five pi over six to seven pi over six, and from eleven pi over six back to two pi. The green arcs mark them.
<curious>Add the angular widths. The first is pi over six, the middle is two pi over six, and the last is pi over six again. Together they make four pi over six, which is two pi over three.
The favourable angle is two pi over three and the full circle is two pi. Divide, and the fraction is exactly one third. Clean and exact.
The whole trick lived in one idea: equal angles take equal times, so reason about time on the phase circle rather than reaching for a formula.

And why not one half, the naive guess? Because the particle moves fastest right near the mean, so it lingers less per centimetre there; the central band, though it looks generous, claims only a third of the time.

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Where marks quietly leak away
Never drop the minus sign in $a=-\omega^2 x$; without it you describe a runaway, not an oscillation.
Do not confuse fastest with most accelerated: at the mean, speed is max but acceleration is zero; at the extremes it is the reverse.
Not every periodic motion is SHM. The Earth orbiting the Sun is periodic but not SHM; a sum of two frequencies is periodic but not SHM.
Keep $\omega$ (rad/s) and $f$ (Hz) distinct; they differ by a factor of 2 pi, and most numerical slips trace back to this.
Pro-tip: use $\omega=a_{\max}/v_{\max}$ and $A=v_{\max}^2/a_{\max}$ directly; never solve simultaneous maxima equations.
For two speeds at two positions, square $v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$ for each and subtract to remove $\omega$.

board_events.latex: \textbf{MAX at MEAN}:\ v_{\max}\ \text{at}\ x=0;\quad a_{\max}\ \text{at}\ x=\pm A

segments.text: Before we wrap this part, let us gather the traps that quietly drain marks, because knowing the trap is half of avoiding it.

First and biggest: never drop the minus sign in acceleration equals minus omega squared x. That minus is the physics; it means restoring. Write it as plus omega squared x and you have described a runaway that flies apart, not an oscillation.

Second, do not confuse fastest with most accelerated. At the mean position the speed is maximum but the acceleration is zero. At the extremes the speed is zero but the acceleration is maximum. They are never large at the same place.

Third, resist calling every periodic motion S H M. The Earth orbiting the Sun repeats, yet it is not simple harmonic. A sum of two different frequencies repeats too, but it is not simple harmonic either. S H M demands a single frequency and a linear restoring force.

Fourth, keep omega and f apart in your head. Omega is in radians per second, f is in hertz, and they differ by a factor of two pi. A huge share of numerical slips are just this factor gone missing, so sanity-check your units.
<whisper>Now the pro-tips. When both maxima are given, use omega equals a-max over v-max and A equals v-max squared over a-max directly. Never sit down to solve two simultaneous equations for them.
And for two speeds at two positions, square the velocity-position relation at each point and subtract. Omega vanishes in a single line, every single time.

<chuckle>Finally, one memory hook for the whole part: MAX at MEAN. Speed is maximum at the mean, acceleration is maximum at the extremes, and acceleration always points home. Carry that and the kinematics is yours.
इस part को wrap करने से पहले, चलो वो traps इकट्ठा कर लें जो चुपचाप marks उड़ा देते हैं, क्योंकि trap को जानना ही उससे बचने का आधा काम है.

पहला और सबसे बड़ा: acceleration बराबर minus omega squared x में minus sign कभी मत गिराओ. वो minus ही physics है; इसका मतलब है restoring. इसे plus omega squared x लिखा तो तुमने एक runaway describe कर दिया जो बिखर जाता है, oscillation नहीं.
दूसरा, fastest और most accelerated को मत उलझाओ. mean position पर speed maximum पर acceleration zero. extremes पर speed zero पर acceleration maximum. दोनों कभी एक ही जगह बड़े नहीं होते.

<whisper>तीसरा, हर periodic motion को S H M मत कह देना. Earth का Sun के around घूमना repeat होता है, फिर भी simple harmonic नहीं. दो अलग frequencies का sum भी repeat होता है, पर वो भी simple harmonic नहीं. S H M माँगता है single frequency और linear restoring force.

चौथा, omega और f को दिमाग़ में अलग रखो. omega radians per second में, f hertz में, और दोनों में two pi का factor का फ़र्क़ है. numerical slips का बड़ा हिस्सा बस यही गायब factor है, तो units से sanity-check करो.
अब pro-tips. जब दोनों maxima दिए हों, omega बराबर a-max over v-max और A बराबर v-max squared over a-max सीधे use करो. उनके लिए दो simultaneous equations कभी मत बैठकर solve करो.
और दो positions पर दो speeds के लिए, हर point पर velocity-position relation square करो और घटाओ. omega एक ही line में गायब हो जाती है, हर बार.

<chuckle>आखिर में, पूरे part के लिए एक memory hook: MAX at MEAN. speed mean पर maximum, acceleration extremes पर maximum, और acceleration हमेशा home की तरफ point करती है. इतना याद रखो और kinematics तुम्हारी है.

sections.title: Energy in SHM changes costume

board_events.text: Motion becomes position, and position becomes motion
A marble in a smooth bowl whizzes fastest at the bottom and freezes for an instant at the top of each climb.
Nothing is lost; the energy simply changes costume, motion (kinetic) at the bottom, position (potential) at the top.

board_events.text: At the mean $x=0$: all kinetic, $U=0$. At the extremes $x=\pm A$: all potential, $K=0$.
The restoring force is conservative, so K and U trade off, one rising exactly as the other falls.
Picture a fixed savings split: a spendable current account (K) and a locked deposit (U); money shuttles, net worth is fixed.

segments.text: In the last part energy hardly appeared; now it takes centre stage. Picture a marble rolling back and forth inside a smooth steel bowl, a katori.
At the very bottom it whizzes through fastest. As it climbs the side it slows, stops for an instant at the highest point it reaches, then rolls straight back down.

<curious>Now ask the key question: where did its speed go at the top, and where did it come from at the bottom? Nothing was lost. The energy simply changed costume, wearing motion at the bottom and position at the top.
The picture shows it. At the bottom the marble carries pure kinetic energy; at the rim it carries pure potential energy; and everywhere in between the two share the load.
That sharing has a name and a value. The total mechanical energy, kinetic plus potential, stays fixed at one half k A squared. It never changes as the particle moves.

Pin the two endpoints down. At the mean position the particle is fastest, so the energy is entirely kinetic and the potential is zero. At the extremes it is momentarily frozen, so the energy is entirely potential and the kinetic is zero.
This works only because the restoring force is conservative. Between the extremes, kinetic and potential trade off smoothly, one rising by exactly the amount the other falls.

Here is a homely picture. Imagine a fixed savings of ten thousand rupees split between a current account you can spend instantly, that is kinetic energy, and a locked fixed deposit, that is potential energy. Money shuttles between them, but your net worth never budges.
पिछले part में energy मुश्किल से दिखी; अब वो centre stage पर है. सोचो एक marble एक smooth steel bowl, यानी katori, के अंदर आगे पीछे लुढ़क रहा है.
बिलकुल नीचे वो सबसे fast निकलता है. side चढ़ते हुए slow होता है, ऊँचाई पर पल भर रुकता है, फिर सीधे वापस नीचे लुढ़क आता है.
<curious>अब key सवाल: top पर उसकी speed कहाँ गई, और bottom पर कहाँ से आई? कुछ भी lost नहीं हुआ. energy ने बस costume बदला, bottom पर motion और top पर position पहनकर.
Picture यही दिखाती है. bottom पर marble के पास pure kinetic energy है; rim पर pure potential energy; और बीच में हर जगह दोनों load बाँट लेते हैं.
इस बँटवारे का एक नाम और एक value है. total mechanical energy, kinetic plus potential, fixed रहती है one half k A squared पर. particle के चलने पर भी ये कभी नहीं बदलती.
दोनों endpoints पक्के करो. mean position पर particle सबसे fast है, तो energy पूरी kinetic और potential zero. extremes पर वो पल भर frozen है, तो energy पूरी potential और kinetic zero.
ये सिर्फ़ इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि restoring force conservative है. extremes के बीच kinetic और potential smoothly trade off करते हैं, एक उतना ही बढ़ता है जितना दूसरा घटता है.

एक घरेलू picture. सोचो ten thousand rupees की fixed saving, बँटी हुई एक current account में जो तुरंत खर्च हो, यानी kinetic energy, और एक locked fixed deposit में, यानी potential energy. पैसा इनके बीच shuttle करता है, पर net worth कभी नहीं हिलती.

sections.title: Two consequences the exams test endlessly

board_events.text: Square-law energy and the double-frequency blink

board_events.caption: K and U trade off with position while the total stays flat

board_events.text: Total energy goes as the square of amplitude: double $A$ and the energy quadruples.
In one to-and-fro the particle passes the fast mean twice and the frozen extremes twice, so the energies peak twice.
$E=\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$ holds only for conservative, undamped SHM; friction leaks energy and amplitude decays.
$U$ is measured from a chosen zero, conventionally $U=0$ at the mean; a different reference just adds a constant.

segments.text: Two consequences flow from that fixed total, and the examiner tests them again and again, so let us make both reflexes.
First look at the energy-versus-position picture. The potential rises as an upward parabola, the kinetic falls as a downward one, and their sum is the flat line across the top, the constant total E.

The first consequence hides in that flat line. Because the total is one half k A squared, energy depends on the square of the amplitude. Double the amplitude and the energy does not double, it quadruples.
Say it as a proportionality: E is proportional to A squared. This one line answers a whole family of amplitude-changed questions.

The second consequence is about timing. In a single full to-and-fro, the particle races through the fast mean position twice and freezes at the two extremes twice, so each energy peaks twice per period.

<excited>So the energies blink at twice the oscillation frequency. Kinetic and potential energy each oscillate at two f, with period T over two, even though the displacement itself has period T. Students forget this under pressure, so make it automatic.

One caution. The clean result, energy equals one half k A squared, holds only while the force is conservative and undamped. Add friction and energy leaks away, the amplitude decays, and so does the total.

And one convention. Potential energy is measured from a chosen zero, which we take at the mean position. Pick a different reference and you simply add a constant to U and to E; every difference and all the physics stay the same.
उस fixed total से दो consequences निकलते हैं, और examiner इन्हें बार बार test करता है, तो दोनों को reflex बना लेते हैं.
पहले energy-versus-position picture देखो. potential एक upward parabola की तरह बढ़ती है, kinetic एक downward की तरह गिरती है, और इनका sum है top पर वो flat line, constant total E.
पहला consequence उसी flat line में छुपा है. चूँकि total है one half k A squared, energy amplitude के square पर depend करती है. amplitude दुगुनी करो तो energy दुगुनी नहीं, चौगुनी होती है.
<excited>इसे proportionality में कहो: E, A squared के proportional है. यही एक line amplitude-changed questions का पूरा परिवार हल कर देती है.

दूसरा consequence timing के बारे में है. एक पूरे to-and-fro में particle fast mean position से दो बार गुज़रती है और दोनों extremes पर दो बार freeze होती है, तो हर energy period में दो बार peak करती है.

तो energies oscillation frequency से दुगुनी rate पर blink करती हैं. kinetic और potential energy हर एक two f पर oscillate करती हैं, period T over two के साथ, जबकि displacement का period T है. students pressure में ये भूल जाते हैं, तो इसे automatic बना लो.
एक caution. साफ़ result, energy बराबर one half k A squared, सिर्फ़ तब तक टिकता है जब force conservative और undamped हो. friction डालो तो energy leak होती है, amplitude decay होती है, और total भी.

और एक convention. potential energy एक chosen zero से measure होती है, जो हम mean position पर लेते हैं. दूसरा reference चुनो तो बस U और E में एक constant जुड़ता है; हर difference और सारी physics वही रहती है.

board_events.text: Displacement oscillates at $f$; both $K$ and $U$ oscillate at $2f$ because they carry $\cos^2$ and $\sin^2$ terms.

segments.text: Now the compact formula board for energy. Everything here follows from omega squared equals k over m, plus the kinematics of the last part.

Kinetic energy is one half m v squared. Using velocity equals omega root A squared minus x squared, it becomes one half m omega squared, times the quantity A squared minus x squared. It is largest at the mean.
Potential energy is one half k x squared, which is the same as one half m omega squared x squared. It is largest at the extremes and zero at the mean.
Add them and the total is one half k A squared, equivalently one half m omega squared A squared. Notice it carries no x and no t; it is a pure constant.
The bars make the split concrete. Read them left to right: at the mean all green, all kinetic; at the extreme all amber, all potential; and at A over root two the bar splits exactly in half.

Three ratios save enormous time. Kinetic over total is one minus x squared over A squared. Potential over total is x squared over A squared. And kinetic over potential is A squared minus x squared, over x squared.
<whisper>Two landmark facts to carry: kinetic equals potential at x equal to plus or minus A over root two, and the time-average of each energy over a period is exactly E over two.
And keep the frequency fact alive. Displacement oscillates at f, but both energies oscillate at two f, because each carries a cosine-squared or sine-squared term.
अब energy का compact formula board. यहाँ सब कुछ omega squared बराबर k over m, और पिछले part की kinematics से निकलता है.
kinetic energy है one half m v squared. velocity बराबर omega root A squared minus x squared use करके, ये बन जाती है one half m omega squared, times A squared minus x squared. ये mean पर सबसे बड़ी है.
potential energy है one half k x squared, जो one half m omega squared x squared के बराबर है. ये extremes पर सबसे बड़ी और mean पर zero है.
दोनों जोड़ो तो total है one half k A squared, यानी one half m omega squared A squared. ध्यान दो इसमें न x है न t; ये pure constant है.
bars इस बँटवारे को ठोस बना देते हैं. left to right पढ़ो: mean पर पूरा green, पूरा kinetic; extreme पर पूरा amber, पूरा potential; और A over root two पर bar ठीक आधों में बँट जाता है.

<whisper>तीन ratios बहुत time बचाते हैं. kinetic over total है one minus x squared over A squared. potential over total है x squared over A squared. और kinetic over potential है A squared minus x squared, over x squared.
दो landmark facts साथ रखो: kinetic बराबर potential x बराबर plus या minus A over root two पर, और period पर हर energy का time-average exactly E over two.
और frequency वाला fact ज़िंदा रखो. displacement f पर oscillate करती है, पर दोनों energies two f पर, क्योंकि हर एक cosine-squared या sine-squared term रखती है.

sections.title: Derivation: total energy equals half k A squared

board_events.text: Adding K and U cancels the time
Take $x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$ under a conservative force, with $U=0$ at the mean.

board_events.caption: K and U each swing, but their sum is a flat line at E

board_events.text: Every trace of time vanishes: for a conservative force the see-saw between $K$ and $U$ is perfectly balanced.

segments.text: Here is the C B S E board derivation of the total energy, a standard three-mark question. The whole trick is that adding the two energies makes time disappear.
Start from displacement equals A sine of omega t plus phi, under the conservative restoring force, with potential energy set to zero at the mean position.
For the kinetic energy, use velocity equals A omega cosine. One half m v squared becomes one half k A squared, times cosine squared of the phase, once we use m omega squared equals k.
For the potential energy, integrate the restoring force from zero to x. The work stored is one half k x squared, which is one half k A squared, times sine squared of the phase.
Look at the picture before adding. The kinetic curve and the potential curve each swing up and down over the period, but watch their sum, the flat dashed line sitting at E.
Now add them algebraically. The common factor one half k A squared comes out, and inside the bracket we have cosine squared plus sine squared of the same angle.
<chuckle>And that bracket is just one, by the Pythagorean identity. So the total energy is one half k A squared, equivalently one half m omega squared A squared. Every trace of time has vanished.
That is exactly what a conservative force promises. The see-saw between kinetic and potential is so perfectly balanced that their sum stands still even while each one swings.
ये रही total energy की C B S E board derivation, एक standard three-mark question. पूरी trick यही है कि दोनों energies जोड़ने पर time गायब हो जाता है.
displacement बराबर A sine of omega t plus phi से शुरू करो, conservative restoring force के under, potential energy को mean position पर zero रखते हुए.
kinetic energy के लिए velocity बराबर A omega cosine use करो. one half m v squared बन जाती है one half k A squared, times cosine squared of the phase, जब हम m omega squared बराबर k लगाते हैं.
potential energy के लिए restoring force को zero से x तक integrate करो. stored work है one half k x squared, यानी one half k A squared, times sine squared of the phase.
जोड़ने से पहले picture देखो. kinetic curve और potential curve हर एक period में ऊपर नीचे झूलती हैं, पर इनका sum देखो, वो flat dashed line E पर बैठी हुई.
<chuckle>अब algebra में जोड़ो. common factor one half k A squared बाहर आता है, और bracket के अंदर है उसी angle का cosine squared plus sine squared.
और वो bracket तो बस one है, Pythagorean identity से. तो total energy है one half k A squared, यानी one half m omega squared A squared. time का हर निशान गायब हो गया.
यही तो conservative force का वादा है. kinetic और potential के बीच का see-saw इतना perfectly balanced है कि उनका sum स्थिर रहता है, जबकि हर एक झूलती रहती है.

sections.title: Derivation: why the energies run at double frequency

board_events.text: Power-reduction reveals the $2\omega$ hidden inside
Apply the power-reduction identities to the $\cos^2$ and $\sin^2$ terms.

board_events.caption: Displacement completes one cycle in T; kinetic energy completes two

board_events.text: Each energy is a constant $E/2$ plus a part oscillating at $2\omega$, so its period is $T/2$.
The oscillating parts are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the sum, leaving $E$ constant.

segments.text: The last derivation proved the sum is constant. This one exposes the timing, and it explains the double-frequency fact that trips so many students.
Take the kinetic energy, which carries a cosine squared, and the potential energy, which carries a sine squared, and rewrite both with the power-reduction identities.

The identities are standard. Cosine squared theta is one plus cosine two theta, all over two. Sine squared theta is one minus cosine two theta, all over two. Notice the angle has doubled to two theta.
Substitute into the kinetic energy. It becomes E over two, plus E over two times cosine of two times the phase. A constant part, and a wiggling part at the doubled angle.
Do the same for the potential energy. It becomes E over two, minus E over two times cosine of the same doubled angle. Same constant, opposite wiggle.
The picture nails it. Displacement completes exactly one cycle in the period T. The kinetic energy, sitting below, completes two full humps in that same time, so its frequency is doubled.
So each energy is a fixed E over two, plus a term oscillating at two omega. That doubled angular frequency means a period of T over two, half the displacement period.

<excited>And notice the bonus. The two wiggling parts are equal and opposite, so when you add kinetic and potential they cancel exactly, leaving the constant E, just as the previous derivation demanded.
पिछली derivation ने साबित किया कि sum constant है. ये वाली timing उजागर करती है, और वही double-frequency fact समझाती है जिस पर बहुत students फिसलते हैं.
kinetic energy लो, जो cosine squared रखती है, और potential energy, जो sine squared रखती है, और दोनों को power-reduction identities से दोबारा लिखो.

identities standard हैं. cosine squared theta है one plus cosine two theta, पूरा over two. sine squared theta है one minus cosine two theta, पूरा over two. ध्यान दो angle दुगुना होकर two theta हो गया.
kinetic energy में substitute करो. ये बन जाती है E over two, plus E over two times cosine of two times the phase. एक constant हिस्सा, और एक wiggling हिस्सा दुगुने angle पर.
यही potential energy के साथ करो. ये बन जाती है E over two, minus E over two times cosine उसी दुगुने angle का. वही constant, उल्टा wiggle.
<excited>Picture इसे पक्का कर देती है. displacement period T में ठीक एक cycle पूरा करती है. kinetic energy, नीचे बैठी, उसी समय में दो पूरे humps पूरे करती है, तो इसकी frequency दुगुनी है.
तो हर energy है एक fixed E over two, plus एक term जो two omega पर oscillate करती है. वो दुगुनी angular frequency मतलब period T over two, displacement period का आधा.
और bonus देखो. दोनों wiggling हिस्से equal और opposite हैं, तो kinetic और potential जोड़ने पर वो exactly cancel हो जाते हैं, बचता है constant E, जैसा पिछली derivation ने माँगा था.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): energy of a block on a spring

board_events.text: Total energy, then the maxima and the top speed
Given: mass 0.5 kg, force constant 200 N/m, amplitude 4 cm. Find $E$, max $K$, max $U$, max speed.
Max KE is at the mean where all energy is kinetic; max PE is at the extremes where all is potential.
Find the total first, then read the maxima straight off it: the mean gives all $K$, the extremes all $U$.
Answer: $E = K_{\max} = U_{\max} = 0.16$ J and $v_{\max} = 0.8$ m/s.

segments.text: A clean C B S E numerical to make the formulas concrete. A block on a frictionless spring is set oscillating, and we want its energy budget.
The data: the mass is zero point five kilograms, the force constant is two hundred newtons per metre, and the amplitude is four centimetres, which is zero point zero four metres.

Start with the total energy, one half k A squared. That is one half times two hundred times zero point zero four squared, which is one hundred times zero point zero zero one six, giving zero point one six joules.
Now use the locations. Maximum kinetic energy sits at the mean, where all the energy is kinetic. Maximum potential energy sits at the extremes, where all the energy is potential.
So both maxima simply equal the total. Maximum kinetic energy and maximum potential energy are each zero point one six joules, the same as E.

For the top speed, set one half m v-max squared equal to the total energy. Rearranging, v-max is the square root of two E over m, the square root of two times zero point one six over zero point five, which is root zero point six four, or zero point eight metres per second.
<chuckle>See the rhythm that scores full marks: compute the total energy first, then read the maxima straight off it. The mean gives you all kinetic, the extremes all potential, no extra work.
So the answer, tidied up: the total energy, the maximum kinetic, and the maximum potential are all zero point one six joules, and the maximum speed is zero point eight metres per second.
एक साफ़ C B S E numerical, formulas को ठोस बनाने के लिए. एक frictionless spring पर block oscillate कराया गया है, और हमें उसका energy budget चाहिए.
data: mass zero point five kilograms, force constant two hundred newtons per metre, और amplitude four centimetres, यानी zero point zero four metres.

total energy से शुरू करो, one half k A squared. वो है one half times two hundred times zero point zero four squared, यानी one hundred times zero point zero zero one six, जो देता है zero point one six joules.
अब locations use करो. maximum kinetic energy mean पर है, जहाँ पूरी energy kinetic है. maximum potential energy extremes पर है, जहाँ पूरी energy potential है.
<chuckle>तो दोनों maxima बस total के बराबर हैं. maximum kinetic energy और maximum potential energy हर एक zero point one six joules, E जितनी.

top speed के लिए one half m v-max squared को total energy के बराबर रखो. rearrange करो तो v-max है square root of two E over m, यानी square root of two times zero point one six over zero point five, जो root zero point six four, या zero point eight metres per second है.
वो rhythm देखो जो full marks दिलाती है: पहले total energy निकालो, फिर maxima उससे सीधे पढ़ लो. mean देता है पूरा kinetic, extremes पूरा potential, कोई extra काम नहीं.
तो answer, साफ़ करके: total energy, maximum kinetic, और maximum potential सब zero point one six joules, और maximum speed zero point eight metres per second.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): where kinetic equals potential

board_events.text: Not at A over two, but at A over root two
At what displacement, as a fraction of amplitude, does $K=U$?
The tempting wrong answer is $x=A/2$; but energy goes as $x^2$, so the split happens later.

board_events.caption: K and U cross at x = plus or minus A over root two, each equal to E over two

board_events.text: At this point each energy is exactly half the total, $E/2$.
Cousins worth memorising: $U=E/4$ at $x=A/2$, and $U=\tfrac{3}{4}E$ at $x=\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}A$.

segments.text: This N E E T favourite is asked almost every year, and it hinges on resisting one very tempting guess.
The question is simple: at what displacement, expressed as a fraction of the amplitude, are the kinetic and potential energies exactly equal?

Here is the trap. The instinctive answer is x equals A over two, halfway out. But halfway in displacement is not halfway in energy, because energy grows as the square of displacement, so the split happens later than you would guess.

Do it honestly. Set kinetic equal to potential: one half k times A squared minus x squared, equals one half k x squared. The halves and the k cancel, leaving A squared minus x squared equals x squared.
Solve. Two x squared equals A squared, so x is A over root two, about zero point seven zero seven times the amplitude. Noticeably past the halfway mark, exactly as the square law warned.
The picture confirms it. The falling kinetic curve and the rising potential curve cross not at A over two but out at A over root two, and they cross at height E over two.
<curious>So at that special position each energy is exactly half the total, E over two. That is the whole content of the result, and it is worth burning into memory.

Two cousins ride along for free. At x equal to A over two the potential is E over four, and at x equal to root three over two times A the potential is three quarters of E. Handy checkpoints for objective questions.
ये N E E T favourite लगभग हर साल पूछा जाता है, और ये एक बहुत tempting guess से बचने पर टिका है.
सवाल simple है: किस displacement पर, amplitude के fraction में, kinetic और potential energies exactly बराबर होती हैं?

<curious>यही रहा trap. सहज answer है x बराबर A over two, आधा बाहर. पर displacement में आधा होना energy में आधा होना नहीं है, क्योंकि energy displacement के square पर बढ़ती है, तो split बाद में होता है.
ईमानदारी से करो. kinetic को potential के बराबर रखो: one half k times A squared minus x squared, बराबर one half k x squared. halves और k cancel, बचता है A squared minus x squared बराबर x squared.
solve करो. two x squared बराबर A squared, तो x है A over root two, लगभग zero point seven zero seven times amplitude. halfway mark से साफ़ आगे, बिलकुल जैसा square law ने चेताया.
picture इसे confirm करती है. गिरती kinetic curve और चढ़ती potential curve A over two पर नहीं बल्कि बाहर A over root two पर cross करती हैं, और वो E over two की height पर cross करती हैं.
तो उस special position पर हर energy exactly total की आधी, E over two. यही पूरे result का सार है, और इसे memory में जला लेना चाहिए.

दो cousins मुफ़्त में साथ आते हैं. x बराबर A over two पर potential E over four है, और x बराबर root three over two times A पर potential three quarters of E है. objective questions के लिए handy checkpoints.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): split the energy at a point

board_events.text: Total first, then divide by position
Given: mass 0.1 kg, amplitude 10 cm, angular frequency 10 rad/s. Find $K$ and $U$ at 6 cm.
Cross-check: 0.032 over 0.018 is 16 over 9. Consistent.
Compute the total first, then split by position; never integrate from scratch each time.

segments.text: A J E E Main numerical that rewards a tidy order of operations: total energy first, then split it using the position.

The data: the mass is zero point one kilograms, the amplitude is ten centimetres, and the angular frequency is ten radians per second. We want the kinetic and potential energies when the particle is six centimetres from the mean.
Total energy is one half m omega squared A squared. That is one half times zero point one, times one hundred, times zero point zero one, which comes to zero point zero five joules.

Potential energy at the given point is one half m omega squared x squared. Put x equal to zero point zero six metres: one half times zero point one, times one hundred, times zero point zero zero three six, giving zero point zero one eight joules.
Kinetic energy is then just the total minus the potential. Zero point zero five minus zero point zero one eight is zero point zero three two joules. No new integration needed.

Now verify with the position ratio. Kinetic over potential is A squared minus x squared, over x squared, which is one hundred minus thirty six, over thirty six, that is sixty four over thirty six, or sixteen over nine.
<chuckle>Cross-check against the numbers: zero point zero three two divided by zero point zero one eight is indeed sixteen over nine. The two routes agree, so we can trust the answer.
The takeaway is the order: compute the total energy once, then split it by position using the ready ratios. Never grind through the integral from scratch every time.
एक J E E Main numerical जो साफ़ order of operations को इनाम देता है: पहले total energy, फिर position से split.
data: mass zero point one kilograms, amplitude ten centimetres, और angular frequency ten radians per second. हमें kinetic और potential energies चाहिए जब particle mean से six centimetres दूर है.
total energy है one half m omega squared A squared. वो है one half times zero point one, times one hundred, times zero point zero one, जो बनता है zero point zero five joules.

दिए point पर potential energy है one half m omega squared x squared. x बराबर zero point zero six metres रखो: one half times zero point one, times one hundred, times zero point zero zero three six, यानी zero point zero one eight joules.
<chuckle>kinetic energy फिर बस total minus potential है. zero point zero five minus zero point zero one eight है zero point zero three two joules. कोई नई integration नहीं.

अब position ratio से verify करो. kinetic over potential है A squared minus x squared, over x squared, यानी one hundred minus thirty six, over thirty six, यानी sixty four over thirty six, या sixteen over nine.
numbers से cross-check: zero point zero three two divided by zero point zero one eight सचमुच sixteen over nine है. दोनों routes agree करते हैं, तो answer पर भरोसा कर सकते हैं.
सीख है order में: total energy एक बार निकालो, फिर ready ratios से position के हिसाब से split करो. हर बार integral शुरू से मत घिसो.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): two kinds of average

board_events.text: Averaged over time versus averaged over position
Show the time-averaged $K$ over a period is $E/2$, but the average over position is $2E/3$.

board_events.caption: Time weighting sits at E over two; position weighting rises to two E over three

board_events.text: The particle moves slowly near the extremes where $K$ is small, so it lingers in low-$K$ regions.
Time-weighting drags the mean to $E/2$; position-weighting treats every centimetre equally, giving $2E/3$.
The lesson: average is meaningless until you say averaged with respect to what.

segments.text: A genuine J E E Advanced trap now, and it is more about clear thinking than heavy calculation. The same kinetic energy can have two different averages, and we must find both.
The claim: averaged over time across one period, the kinetic energy is E over two. But averaged over position from minus A to plus A, it is two E over three. Different numbers, same energy.

Take the time average first. Kinetic energy is E cosine squared of omega t. Average cosine squared over a full period and you get one half, so the time-averaged kinetic energy is E times one half, that is E over two.

Now the position average. Write kinetic energy as E over A squared, times the quantity A squared minus x squared, and average it uniformly over x from minus A to A. The integral works out to two E over three.
The picture explains the gap. Two levels are drawn on the same kinetic-energy curve: the time average sits lower, at E over two, and the position average sits higher, at two E over three.
<curious>Why the difference? The particle moves slowly near the extremes, where kinetic energy is small, so it lingers there and spends extra time in low-kinetic regions.

So time-weighting, which counts every second the particle actually spends, is dragged down to E over two. Position-weighting treats every centimetre of the path equally, regardless of how long the particle dawdles there, and comes out higher at two E over three.
The deeper lesson is worth more than the numbers: an average is meaningless until you say averaged with respect to what. Time and position give genuinely different answers.
अब एक असली J E E Advanced trap, और ये heavy calculation से ज़्यादा साफ़ सोच के बारे में है. एक ही kinetic energy के दो अलग averages हो सकते हैं, और हमें दोनों निकालने हैं.
claim: एक period पर time के हिसाब से average करो तो kinetic energy E over two. पर minus A से plus A तक position के हिसाब से average करो तो two E over three. अलग numbers, वही energy.
पहले time average लो. kinetic energy है E cosine squared of omega t. पूरे period पर cosine squared का average one half होता है, तो time-averaged kinetic energy है E times one half, यानी E over two.
अब position average. kinetic energy को E over A squared, times A squared minus x squared लिखो, और x को minus A से A तक uniformly average करो. integral निकलता है two E over three.
<curious>picture gap समझाती है. एक ही kinetic-energy curve पर दो levels खींचे हैं: time average नीचे, E over two पर, और position average ऊपर, two E over three पर.
फ़र्क़ क्यों? particle extremes के पास slowly चलती है, जहाँ kinetic energy छोटी है, तो वहाँ ज़्यादा रुकती है और low-kinetic regions में extra time बिताती है.

तो time-weighting, जो particle के सचमुच बिताए हर second को गिनती है, नीचे E over two तक खिंच जाती है. position-weighting हर centimetre को बराबर मानती है, चाहे particle वहाँ कितना भी रुके, और ऊपर two E over three पर आती है.
गहरी सीख numbers से ज़्यादा कीमती है: average तब तक meaningless है जब तक तुम न कहो किसके respect में average. time और position सचमुच अलग answers देते हैं.

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: The four traps that cost energy marks
Both $K$ and $U$ oscillate at $2f$ (period $T/2$), not at $f$; the particle passes the mean twice and the extremes twice per cycle.
$K=U$ happens at $x=A/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.707A$, noticeably past the halfway mark, not at $A/2$.
Write $E\propto A^2$, never $E\propto A$; always square the amplitude ratio in amplitude-changed problems.
Time-averaged $K$ and $U$ are each $E/2$, but that does not mean $K=U$ at every instant.
Pro-tip: use the ready ratios $K/E = 1 - x^2/A^2$ and $U/E = x^2/A^2$ directly instead of re-deriving.
Between the crossover point and the square law, you answer most objective questions on this subtopic.

segments.text: Before we close SHM energy, let us round up the four traps that quietly cost marks, because each one is a habit you can fix in a minute.

First and most forgotten: both kinetic and potential energy oscillate at two f, with period T over two, not at f. The particle passes the fast mean twice and the frozen extremes twice in every cycle, so the energies peak twice.

Second, do not put kinetic equals potential at x equal to A over two. Energy goes as x squared, so the equality lands at A over root two, about zero point seven zero seven of the amplitude, noticeably past the halfway mark.
Third, write energy proportional to A squared, never proportional to A. In any amplitude-changed problem, always square the amplitude ratio; forgetting to square is a huge source of lost marks.

Fourth, remember that time-averaged kinetic and potential are each E over two, but that is an average. It does not mean the two are equal at every instant; they are equal only at the special points, plus or minus A over root two.

<whisper>Now a pro-tip that saves real time. Do not re-derive energies at a given position. Use the ready ratios directly: kinetic over total is one minus x squared over A squared, and potential over total is x squared over A squared.
Lock in the two landmarks that carry this subtopic: kinetic equals potential at A over root two, and total energy is proportional to A squared.
<chuckle>Between those two facts, the crossover point and the square law, you can answer the large majority of objective questions this subtopic ever throws at you.
SHM energy बंद करने से पहले, चलो वो चार traps इकट्ठा कर लें जो चुपचाप marks खा जाते हैं, क्योंकि हर एक एक आदत है जो एक मिनट में सुधर सकती है.

पहला और सबसे भूला हुआ: kinetic और potential energy दोनों two f पर oscillate करती हैं, period T over two के साथ, f पर नहीं. particle हर cycle में fast mean से दो बार और frozen extremes पर दो बार गुज़रती है, तो energies दो बार peak करती हैं.

<whisper>दूसरा, kinetic बराबर potential को x बराबर A over two पर मत रखो. energy x squared पर जाती है, तो equality A over root two पर आती है, amplitude का लगभग zero point seven zero seven, halfway mark से साफ़ आगे.
तीसरा, energy को A squared के proportional लिखो, कभी A के proportional नहीं. किसी भी amplitude-changed problem में amplitude ratio को हमेशा square करो; square करना भूलना lost marks का बड़ा source है.

चौथा, याद रखो time-averaged kinetic और potential हर एक E over two हैं, पर वो एक average है. इसका मतलब ये नहीं कि दोनों हर पल बराबर हैं; वो सिर्फ़ special points, plus या minus A over root two, पर बराबर हैं.

अब एक pro-tip जो सचमुच time बचाता है. किसी position पर energies दोबारा मत निकालो. ready ratios सीधे use करो: kinetic over total है one minus x squared over A squared, और potential over total है x squared over A squared.
<chuckle>इस subtopic को सँभालने वाले दो landmarks पक्के करो: kinetic बराबर potential A over root two पर, और total energy A squared के proportional.
उन दो facts के बीच, crossover point और square law, तुम इस subtopic के फेंके ज़्यादातर objective questions answer कर सकते हो.

board_events.text: Pendulum by gravity, spring by elasticity
Almost every oscillation you will solve is one of two systems in disguise: a pendulum driven by gravity or a mass-spring driven by elasticity.

board_events.text: Pull a pendulum aside; the tangential part of gravity, $mg\sin\theta$, hauls the bob back. For small swings $\sin\theta\approx\theta$, so the force is proportional to displacement: SHM.
The period depends only on length and $g$, not on the mass of the bob nor, for small angles, on the amplitude.
This mass- and amplitude-independence is isochronism, the property Galileo spotted watching a swinging cathedral lamp.
Equal-length pendulums, heavy bob or light, keep perfect time together, which is why pendulum clocks work.

segments.text: There are just two great workhorses of S H M, and almost every oscillation problem you will ever solve is one of them wearing a disguise.

One is the pendulum, driven by gravity; the other is the mass-spring, driven by elasticity. One swings, the other bounces, yet both obey the very same master rule from the first part: a restoring force proportional to displacement.
Look at the two side by side. The pendulum hangs and sweeps an arc; the block sits on a spring and bounces along a line. Different machinery, identical law.

Take the pendulum first. Pull the bob aside and gravity tries to drag it straight down, but the string only lets it move along an arc. The tangential part of gravity, m g sine theta, is what hauls it back. For small swings the sine of theta is nearly theta, so the restoring force becomes proportional to displacement, and that is exactly S H M.
Out of this falls one of the most beautiful results in physics. The period equals two pi times the square root of L over g.
Read what is, and is not, in that formula. The period depends only on the length and on g. It does not depend on the mass of the bob, and for small angles it does not depend on the amplitude either.

<excited>This independence has a name, isochronism, and it is the property Galileo spotted while watching a lamp swing in a cathedral. A heavy bob and a light bob on strings of equal length keep perfect time together.
That single fact is the reason pendulum clocks can keep time at all. Length and gravity set the beat; nothing else gets a vote.
S H M के बस दो बड़े workhorses हैं, और लगभग हर oscillation problem जो तुम कभी solve करोगे इन्हीं में से एक है, disguise पहने हुए.

एक है pendulum, gravity से चलने वाला; दूसरा है mass-spring, elasticity से चलने वाला. एक swing करता है, दूसरा bounce, फिर भी दोनों वही master rule मानते हैं: restoring force displacement के proportional.
दोनों को साथ देखो. pendulum लटककर arc बनाता है; block spring पर बैठकर एक line में bounce करता है. अलग machinery, वही law.

<excited>पहले pendulum. bob को एक तरफ खींचो तो gravity उसे सीधे नीचे खींचना चाहती है, पर string उसे सिर्फ़ arc पर चलने देती है. gravity का tangential हिस्सा, m g sine theta, ही उसे वापस खींचता है. small swings पर sine theta लगभग theta है, तो restoring force displacement के proportional बन जाती है, और यही तो S H M है.
इसी से physics का एक सबसे सुंदर result निकलता है. period बराबर two pi times square root of L over g.
पढ़ो उस formula में क्या है और क्या नहीं. period सिर्फ़ length और g पर depend करता है. ये bob के mass पर नहीं, और small angles पर amplitude पर भी नहीं.
इस independence का एक नाम है, isochronism, और यही वो property है जो Galileo ने cathedral में lamp झूलते देखकर पकड़ी थी. बराबर length की strings पर heavy और light bob perfect time साथ रखते हैं.
यही एक fact pendulum clocks के time रखने की वजह है. length और gravity beat तय करते हैं; और किसी की नहीं चलती.

sections.title: Why mass cancels for a pendulum but rules the spring

board_events.text: Same rule, opposite dependence on mass and gravity

board_events.caption: On the Moon a pendulum slows; the spring keeps the same period

board_events.text: In a pendulum a heavier bob feels more gravity but is also more sluggish; the two cancel exactly, so mass drops out.
In a spring the elastic force is set by stiffness $k$ alone; a heavier mass only adds inertia, so the period grows.
A spring-mass system has the same period on the Moon; a pendulum would slow. Gravity only shifts a vertical spring's mean.
Pendulum SHM needs small angles ($\theta$ under about ten degrees); larger swings make the period grow with amplitude.
The ideal pendulum is a point bob on a massless string; a real rod is a physical pendulum with a different formula.

segments.text: Here is a question that separates real understanding from rote learning: why does the mass cancel for a pendulum but matter for a spring? The answer is different in each case, and it is worth savouring.
The picture sets the contrast. Take both systems to the Moon. The pendulum, feeling weaker gravity, slows right down. The spring keeps exactly the same period.

For the pendulum, think about the two roles mass plays. A heavier bob feels a stronger pull, more gravity driving it, but it is also more sluggish, more inertia resisting it. The two effects scale together and cancel exactly, so mass drops clean out of the period.

For the spring the story runs the other way. The elastic force is set by the stiffness k alone; it does not care how much mass hangs on it. So a heavier mass just adds inertia with no extra force to compensate, and the period grows.
Hence the spring period is two pi root m over k, and, strikingly, it contains no g at all.

<curious>That is the favourite trap. Hang the same spring-mass system on the Moon and it oscillates with exactly the same period, while the pendulum slows down. For a vertical spring, gravity only shifts the mean position downward; it never touches the period.

Two cautions frame all of this. The pendulum is simple harmonic only for small angles, roughly under ten degrees, where the sine of theta is nearly theta. At large swings the period starts to grow with amplitude.
And the ideal pendulum is a point-mass bob on a massless, inextensible string. A real rod or extended body is a physical pendulum, which we will meet with its own formula.
एक सवाल जो असली समझ को rote से अलग करता है: pendulum के लिए mass cancel क्यों होती है पर spring के लिए matter करती है? जवाब हर case में अलग है, और मज़ा लेने लायक है.
picture contrast दिखाती है. दोनों systems को Moon पर ले जाओ. pendulum, कमज़ोर gravity महसूस करके, धीमा हो जाता है. spring बिलकुल वही period रखता है.

pendulum के लिए mass की दो भूमिकाएँ सोचो. heavier bob को ज़्यादा pull मिलता है, ज़्यादा gravity धकेलती है, पर वो ज़्यादा sluggish भी है, ज़्यादा inertia रोकती है. दोनों effects साथ scale करके exactly cancel हो जाते हैं, तो mass period से साफ़ निकल जाती है.

<curious>spring में कहानी उल्टी चलती है. elastic force सिर्फ़ stiffness k से तय होती है; उसे परवाह नहीं कितनी mass लटकी है. तो heavier mass बस inertia जोड़ती है, compensate करने को कोई extra force नहीं, और period बढ़ जाता है.
इसलिए spring period है two pi root m over k, और हैरानी की बात, इसमें g है ही नहीं.

यही favourite trap है. वही spring-mass system Moon पर लटकाओ तो वो बिलकुल उसी period पर oscillate करता है, जबकि pendulum धीमा हो जाता है. vertical spring के लिए gravity सिर्फ़ mean position नीचे खिसकाती है; period को छूती तक नहीं.
दो cautions इस सबको घेरते हैं. pendulum simple harmonic सिर्फ़ small angles पर है, लगभग ten degrees से कम, जहाँ sine theta लगभग theta है. large swings पर period amplitude के साथ बढ़ने लगता है.
और ideal pendulum एक point-mass bob है massless, inextensible string पर. real rod या extended body एक physical pendulum है, जिसे हम उसके अपने formula के साथ मिलेंगे.

sections.title: Formula board, part one: periods and spring combinations

board_events.text: Pendulum, spring, static stretch, and combinations

board_events.caption: Series is softer; parallel is stiffer

board_events.text: Series is softer (longer $T$); parallel stiffer (shorter $T$); a cut piece is stiffer, not weaker.

segments.text: Let us put the working formulas on the board. This subtopic is formula-dense, so we split them into two clean panels.
First the simple pendulum: period two pi root L over g, with angular frequency root g over L. Length and gravity, nothing else.
Then the mass-spring: period two pi root m over k, angular frequency root k over m. Mass and stiffness, and notably no g.

A handy shortcut for a vertical spring. If it hangs stretched by an amount x-nought at equilibrium, then m g equals k x-nought, and the period can be written two pi root x-nought over g. Useful when the mass and stiffness are not given separately.
Now spring combinations, shown in the picture. Stack them in series and the system is softer; place them side by side in parallel and it is stiffer.
In series the reciprocals add: one over k-effective equals one over k-one plus one over k-two. In parallel the constants add directly: k-effective equals k-one plus k-two.
<whisper>And a favourite exam fact: cut a spring into n equal pieces and each piece becomes stiffer, with constant n times k. A shorter spring stretches less under the same force.
Hold the summary. Series is softer and gives a longer period; parallel is stiffer and gives a shorter period; and a cut piece is stiffer, never weaker.
चलो working formulas board पर रख देते हैं. ये subtopic formula-dense है, तो इन्हें दो साफ़ panels में बाँटते हैं.
पहले simple pendulum: period two pi root L over g, angular frequency root g over L. length और gravity, और कुछ नहीं.
फिर mass-spring: period two pi root m over k, angular frequency root k over m. mass और stiffness, और खास बात कोई g नहीं.

vertical spring के लिए एक handy shortcut. अगर वो equilibrium पर x-nought जितना stretched लटका है, तो m g बराबर k x-nought, और period लिखा जा सकता है two pi root x-nought over g. तब काम आता है जब mass और stiffness अलग से न दिए हों.
<whisper>अब spring combinations, picture में दिखाए. series में stack करो तो system softer; parallel में side by side रखो तो stiffer.
series में reciprocals जुड़ते हैं: one over k-effective बराबर one over k-one plus one over k-two. parallel में constants सीधे जुड़ते हैं: k-effective बराबर k-one plus k-two.
और एक favourite exam fact: spring को n equal pieces में काटो तो हर piece stiffer हो जाता है, constant n times k के साथ. छोटी spring उसी force पर कम stretch होती है.
summary पकड़ो. series softer और longer period; parallel stiffer और shorter period; और cut piece stiffer, कभी weaker नहीं.

board_events.text: Free fall ($a=g$) gives $g_{\text{eff}}=0$: the bob floats and never swings.
Here $I$ is the moment of inertia about the pivot and $\kappa$ the restoring torque per unit twist.

segments.text: The second panel handles the trickier settings: pendulums in accelerating frames, and rigid bodies that swing.
The idea for accelerating frames is one substitution: replace the ordinary g by an effective gravity, g-effective, that the bob actually feels. The picture shows the three standard cases.

In a lift accelerating upward, the bob feels heavier, so g-effective is g plus a and the period shortens. In a lift accelerating downward, it feels lighter, so g-effective is g minus a and the period lengthens.

For a car accelerating horizontally, the apparent gravity is the vector sum, so its magnitude is the square root of g squared plus a squared, and the mean position tilts from the vertical by an angle whose tangent is a over g.

For a rigid body swinging about a pivot, the physical pendulum, the period is two pi root I over m g d, where d is the pivot-to-centre-of-mass distance. Its equivalent simple-pendulum length is I over m d.
And a disc on a wire gives the torsional pendulum, with period two pi root I over kappa, where kappa is the torsional constant.

<curious>One limiting case is delicious. In free fall the lift's acceleration equals g, so g-effective is zero, the bob floats, and it never swings at all. The formula predicts an infinite period, and physically the pendulum simply stops.
Keep the symbols straight: I is the moment of inertia about the pivot, and kappa is the restoring torque per unit twist, measured in newton metres per radian.
दूसरा panel मुश्किल settings सँभालता है: accelerating frames में pendulums, और swing करते rigid bodies.
accelerating frames का idea एक substitution है: सामान्य g की जगह एक effective gravity, g-effective, रखो जो bob सचमुच महसूस करता है. picture तीन standard cases दिखाती है.

ऊपर accelerate करते lift में bob भारी महसूस करता है, तो g-effective है g plus a और period छोटा होता है. नीचे accelerate करते lift में हल्का महसूस करता है, तो g-effective है g minus a और period बड़ा होता है.

horizontal accelerate करती car के लिए apparent gravity vector sum है, तो इसका magnitude है square root of g squared plus a squared, और mean position vertical से एक angle पर झुक जाती है जिसका tangent है a over g.

pivot के around swing करते rigid body, यानी physical pendulum, के लिए period है two pi root I over m g d, जहाँ d है pivot-to-centre-of-mass distance. इसकी equivalent simple-pendulum length है I over m d.
<curious>और wire पर disc torsional pendulum देता है, period two pi root I over kappa के साथ, जहाँ kappa torsional constant है.

एक limiting case मज़ेदार है. free fall में lift का acceleration g के बराबर है, तो g-effective zero, bob तैरता है, और swing करता ही नहीं. formula infinite period predict करता है, और physically pendulum बस रुक जाता है.
symbols साफ़ रखो: I है pivot के around moment of inertia, और kappa है per unit twist restoring torque, newton metres per radian में.
