board_events.text: A point bob on a light string of length $L$ is displaced by a small angle $\theta$.
Resolve gravity: $mg\cos\theta$ balances the tension; $mg\sin\theta$ along the arc is the restoring force.
The effective stiffness is $k=mg/L$; comparing with $\omega^2=k/m$ makes the mass cancel.
Gravity, the agent of the restoring force, scales with $m$ exactly as the inertia does, so the bob's weight is irrelevant.

segments.text: Now the C B S E board derivation of the pendulum period, an almost-guaranteed three-mark question. It is our recipe from part one, applied to gravity.
The picture carries the whole idea. Gravity points straight down, but the string forces the bob onto an arc, so we split gravity into two parts, one along the string and one across it.
Set the stage. A point-mass bob hangs on a light, inextensible string of length L, displaced from the vertical by a small angle theta.

Resolve gravity. The component along the string, m g cosine theta, is balanced by the string tension and does no restoring. The component along the arc, m g sine theta, points back toward the lowest point, and that is the restoring force.

Now the small-angle magic. For small theta the sine of theta is nearly theta, and the arc displacement s equals L theta, so theta is s over L. The restoring force becomes minus m g over L, times s, which is exactly the S H M shape, minus a constant times displacement.
Compare with omega squared equals stiffness over mass. The effective stiffness is m g over L, so omega squared is g over L, and the period is two pi root L over g.
<chuckle>Watch the mass vanish. The effective stiffness carried an m, but dividing by the inertial m cancelled it exactly. That is the mathematical face of isochronism.

And the physics behind the cancellation: gravity, which supplies the restoring force, scales with the mass in just the same way as the inertia that resists it, so the bob's weight simply does not matter to its timing.
अब pendulum period की C B S E board derivation, एक लगभग-guaranteed three-mark question. ये part one वाली हमारी recipe है, gravity पर लगाई गई.
picture पूरा idea रखती है. gravity सीधे नीचे point करती है, पर string bob को arc पर मजबूर करती है, तो हम gravity को दो हिस्सों में बाँटते हैं, एक string के साथ और एक उसके across.
stage set करो. एक point-mass bob light, inextensible string, length L, पर लटका है, vertical से small angle theta पर displaced.

gravity resolve करो. string के साथ component, m g cosine theta, string tension से balance होता है और कोई restoring नहीं करता. arc के साथ component, m g sine theta, lowest point की तरफ point करता है, और यही restoring force है.

<chuckle>अब small-angle magic. small theta पर sine theta लगभग theta है, और arc displacement s बराबर L theta, तो theta है s over L. restoring force बन जाती है minus m g over L, times s, जो exactly S H M shape है, minus constant times displacement.
omega squared बराबर stiffness over mass से compare करो. effective stiffness है m g over L, तो omega squared है g over L, और period है two pi root L over g.
mass को गायब होते देखो. effective stiffness में एक m थी, पर inertial m से divide करने पर वो exactly cancel हो गई. यही isochronism का mathematical चेहरा है.
और cancellation के पीछे की physics: gravity, जो restoring force देती है, mass के साथ ठीक उसी तरह scale करती है जैसे उसे रोकने वाली inertia, तो bob के weight का उसके timing से कोई मतलब नहीं.

Gravity merely relocates the mean by $x_0=mg/k$; it leaves the period untouched.
That is why a spring-mass system keeps the same period regardless of $g$, even on the Moon.

segments.text: The second derivation answers a question students always ask: does hanging a spring vertically change its period? The clean answer is no, and here is exactly why.

Start with the easy horizontal case. Displace the block by x on a frictionless surface and the spring pulls back with minus k x directly. That is the S H M form, so omega is root k over m and the period is two pi root m over k.
Now the picture for the vertical spring. Left, the mass hangs at equilibrium, already stretched by an amount x-nought. Right, we have pushed it down a little more by y.
At equilibrium the spring is stretched by x-nought where k x-nought balances the weight, m g. Crucially, we measure the new displacement y from this shifted equilibrium, not from the natural length.

Now write the net force at displacement y. It is m g minus k times the total stretch, x-nought plus y. Group the terms: m g minus k x-nought is zero by the equilibrium condition, leaving simply minus k y.

<excited>So the vertical spring obeys exactly minus k y, the same restoring law as the horizontal one. Its period is the same two pi root m over k. The gravity term was silently cancelled by the initial stretch.
The moral: gravity merely relocates the mean position downward by x-nought equals m g over k. It shifts where the block sits, but it leaves the period completely untouched.
And this is precisely why a spring-mass system keeps the same period regardless of g. Take it to the Moon and the mean position rises, but the beat is unchanged.
दूसरी derivation उस सवाल का जवाब देती है जो students हमेशा पूछते हैं: spring को vertical लटकाने से period बदलता है क्या? साफ़ जवाब है नहीं, और ठीक क्यों, यही देखो.

आसान horizontal case से शुरू करो. frictionless surface पर block को x से displace करो तो spring सीधे minus k x से वापस खींचती है. वही S H M form है, तो omega है root k over m और period two pi root m over k.
अब vertical spring की picture. left, mass equilibrium पर लटकी है, पहले से x-nought जितनी stretched. right, हमने उसे y से थोड़ा और नीचे धकेला है.
equilibrium पर spring x-nought से stretched है जहाँ k x-nought weight, m g, को balance करता है. खास बात, हम नया displacement y इसी shifted equilibrium से measure करते हैं, natural length से नहीं.

<excited>अब y displacement पर net force लिखो. ये है m g minus k times total stretch, x-nought plus y. terms group करो: m g minus k x-nought तो equilibrium condition से zero है, बचता है simply minus k y.
तो vertical spring exactly minus k y मानता है, वही restoring law जो horizontal का. इसका period वही two pi root m over k. gravity term initial stretch से चुपचाप cancel हो गया.
सार: gravity बस mean position को x-nought बराबर m g over k नीचे खिसकाती है. ये तय करती है block कहाँ बैठे, पर period को बिलकुल नहीं छूती.
और ठीक इसीलिए spring-mass system g की परवाह किए बिना वही period रखता है. Moon पर ले जाओ तो mean position ऊपर उठती है, पर beat वही रहती है.

board_events.text: Parallel: both springs stretch by the same $x$, so their forces add.
Series: the same tension $F$ runs through both, so their stretches add.
Parallel springs share the load and act stiffer; series springs each take the full load and act softer.
This is the opposite of how resistors combine, a frequent source of confusion.

segments.text: The third derivation settles series versus parallel springs, and it hinges on asking the right question of each arrangement: what is shared?
The picture makes the distinction crisp. In parallel the two springs share the same stretch; in series they share the same tension.
Take parallel first. Both springs are anchored together and stretch by the same amount x. Each pulls back on its own, so the two forces simply add.
Adding the forces, the total is minus the quantity k-one plus k-two, times x. So the effective constant is k-one plus k-two. Parallel springs are stiffer than either alone.
Now series. The springs are stacked, so the same tension F runs through both, but their stretches add up because each yields a little.

<curious>Write the total stretch as F over k-one plus F over k-two. Since the effective spring would give x equals F over k-effective, comparing gives one over k-effective equals one over k-one plus one over k-two. Series springs are softer.

The physical reading is intuitive. Parallel springs share the load, so together they resist more stiffly. Series springs each take the full tension and each stretches, so the chain is more compliant, softer overall.
One warning worth repeating: this is exactly the opposite of how resistors combine. Do not borrow the resistor rule here, or you will swap stiffer and softer and lose easy marks.

picture फ़र्क़ साफ़ कर देती है. parallel में दोनों springs same stretch share करती हैं; series में same tension.

<curious>अब series. springs stacked हैं, तो same tension F दोनों से गुज़रती है, पर उनके stretches जुड़ते हैं क्योंकि हर एक थोड़ा yield करती है.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): the seconds pendulum

board_events.text: A one-metre pendulum and the square-root length law
A simple pendulum has length 1.0 m. Take $g=\pi^2\approx 9.87$ m/s². Find its period.
A period of 2 s marks a seconds pendulum (each one-way swing takes 1 s); its length is about 1 m.
Now make the length four times as large.
Quadrupling the length doubles the period, because $T\propto\sqrt{L}$.
The seconds pendulum and the square-root length law are both worth memorising outright.

segments.text: A short, satisfying C B S E numerical that also hands you two facts worth memorising for life.
The pendulum has length one point zero metres, and we are told to take g equal to pi squared, which is about nine point eight seven metres per second squared. Find the period.
Substitute into two pi root L over g. That is two pi root one over pi squared, which is two pi times one over pi. The pi cancels neatly, and the period is two seconds.

<chuckle>This is a special one. A pendulum whose period is two seconds is called a seconds pendulum, because each one-way swing takes exactly one second. Notice its length came out at about one metre, which is worth carrying in your head.
Now the second part. Make the length four times as large and see what happens to the period.
Substitute four L into the same formula. The four comes out of the square root as a two, so the new period is two times the old, that is two times two, giving four seconds.
The pattern is the point. Quadrupling the length only doubles the period, because the period goes as the square root of the length. To double the period you must quadruple the length.
So keep both prizes from this example: the seconds pendulum is about one metre long with a two-second period, and period grows as the square root of length.
एक छोटा, संतोषजनक C B S E numerical जो जीवन भर याद रखने लायक दो facts भी देता है.
pendulum की length one point zero metres है, और हमें g बराबर pi squared लेना है, जो लगभग nine point eight seven metres per second squared है. period निकालो.
<chuckle>two pi root L over g में substitute करो. वो है two pi root one over pi squared, यानी two pi times one over pi. pi साफ़ cancel हो जाता है, और period है two seconds.

ये एक खास वाला है. जिस pendulum का period two seconds हो उसे seconds pendulum कहते हैं, क्योंकि हर one-way swing exactly one second लेता है. ध्यान दो इसकी length लगभग one metre निकली, जो दिमाग़ में रखने लायक है.
अब दूसरा हिस्सा. length चार गुना करो और देखो period का क्या होता है.
उसी formula में four L रखो. four square root से बाहर two बनकर आता है, तो नया period है पुराने का two गुना, यानी two times two, यानी four seconds.
pattern ही बात है. length चौगुनी करने पर period सिर्फ़ दुगुना होता है, क्योंकि period length के square root पर जाता है. period दुगुना करने के लिए length चौगुनी करनी पड़ती है.
तो इस example के दोनों इनाम रखो: seconds pendulum लगभग one metre लंबा two-second period के साथ, और period length के square root पर बढ़ता है.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): pendulum in a descending lift

board_events.text: A lighter bob means a longer period
A pendulum has period 2 s in a stationary lift. The lift now accelerates downward at three-quarters $g$. Find the new period.
The trap: a bob in a downward-accelerating lift feels lighter, so effective gravity decreases, not increases.
Use the ratio form so the length cancels; only the gravity ratio matters.
Sanity check: in free fall $a=g$, so $g_{\text{eff}}=0$ and $T'\to\infty$; the bob floats and never swings.
Our answer moves correctly toward that limit as the downward acceleration grows.

segments.text: A neat N E E T application of effective gravity, and a place where the sign trips a lot of students.
The pendulum has a period of two seconds while the lift is stationary. Now the lift accelerates downward at three-quarters of g. Find the new period.

Here is the trap. Some students ignore the lift entirely; others add the acceleration when they should subtract. In a downward-accelerating lift the bob feels lighter, so the effective gravity goes down, not up.
Compute it. The effective gravity is g minus three-quarters g, which is one-quarter g. The bob now behaves as though gravity were only a fourth as strong.

Use the ratio form to avoid needing the length. The ratio of new period to old is the square root of g over g-effective, which is root g over g-over-four, that is root four, which is two. So the new period is two times two, four seconds.
<curious>Notice why the ratio form is smart. Because both periods carry the same length, the length cancels, and only the gravity ratio survives. Less arithmetic, less chance of error.

Now the sanity check that confirms the direction. If the lift were in free fall, the acceleration would equal g, the effective gravity would be zero, and the period would blow up to infinity. The bob floats and never swings.

Our answer sits correctly on the road to that limit: as the downward acceleration grows toward g, the effective gravity shrinks and the period lengthens. Four seconds is exactly the right kind of answer.
effective gravity का एक साफ़ N E E T application, और वो जगह जहाँ sign बहुत students को गिरा देता है.
pendulum का period two seconds है जब lift stationary है. अब lift नीचे three-quarters of g पर accelerate करती है. नया period निकालो.

<curious>यही रहा trap. कुछ students lift को पूरी तरह ignore कर देते हैं; कुछ acceleration add कर देते हैं जब subtract करना चाहिए. नीचे accelerate करती lift में bob हल्का महसूस करता है, तो effective gravity घटती है, बढ़ती नहीं.
इसे निकालो. effective gravity है g minus three-quarters g, यानी one-quarter g. bob अब ऐसे behave करता है मानो gravity सिर्फ़ चौथाई ताक़त की हो.

length की ज़रूरत से बचने को ratio form use करो. नए period का पुराने से ratio है square root of g over g-effective, यानी root g over g-over-four, यानी root four, यानी two. तो नया period है two times two, four seconds.
ध्यान दो ratio form smart क्यों है. चूँकि दोनों periods same length रखते हैं, length cancel हो जाती है, और सिर्फ़ gravity ratio बचता है. कम arithmetic, कम गलती की गुंजाइश.
अब sanity check जो direction confirm करता है. अगर lift free fall में हो, acceleration g के बराबर हो, effective gravity zero हो जाए, और period infinity तक उछल जाए. bob तैरता है और swing करता ही नहीं.
हमारा answer उस limit की तरफ सही रास्ते पर है: जैसे जैसे downward acceleration g की तरफ बढ़ता है, effective gravity घटती है और period बढ़ता है. four seconds बिलकुल सही तरह का answer है.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): springs in series and parallel

board_events.text: Find the effective constant, then the period
A 2 kg block connects to springs of 6 N/m and 3 N/m. Find the period in series and in parallel.
The series combination is softer, so it oscillates more slowly, exactly as intuition predicts.
Find $k_{\text{eff}}$ first, then apply $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k_{\text{eff}}}$; never average the two periods.

segments.text: A bread-and-butter J E E Main problem on spring combinations. The whole method is: get the effective constant first, then drop it into the period formula.
A block of mass two kilograms is connected to two springs, of six newtons per metre and three newtons per metre. Find the period of oscillation in series and in parallel.

Start with series, where the reciprocals add. One over k-effective is one over six plus one over three, which is one over six plus two over six, giving three over six. So k-effective is two newtons per metre.
Put that into the period. Two pi root two over two is two pi root one, just two pi, about six point two eight seconds. A soft combination, a slow oscillation.
Now parallel, where the constants add directly. k-effective is six plus three, which is nine newtons per metre.
<chuckle>Its period is two pi root two over nine, which tidies to two pi root two over three, about two point nine six seconds. Much quicker than the series case.

The comparison is a built-in check on your intuition. The series combination has the smaller effective constant, so it is softer and oscillates more slowly, while the parallel combination is stiffer and faster. That is exactly what we expect.
So the discipline is clear: always find the effective constant first, then apply period equals two pi root m over k-effective. Never try to average the two periods directly, which is meaningless.
spring combinations पर एक bread-and-butter J E E Main problem. पूरा method है: पहले effective constant निकालो, फिर उसे period formula में डालो.
two kilograms mass का block दो springs से जुड़ा है, six newtons per metre और three newtons per metre. series और parallel में oscillation का period निकालो.

series से शुरू करो, जहाँ reciprocals जुड़ते हैं. one over k-effective है one over six plus one over three, यानी one over six plus two over six, यानी three over six. तो k-effective है two newtons per metre.
इसे period में रखो. two pi root two over two है two pi root one, बस two pi, लगभग six point two eight seconds. soft combination, slow oscillation.
<chuckle>अब parallel, जहाँ constants सीधे जुड़ते हैं. k-effective है six plus three, यानी nine newtons per metre.
इसका period है two pi root two over nine, जो साफ़ होकर two pi root two over three, लगभग two point nine six seconds. series case से काफ़ी तेज़.

comparison तुम्हारी intuition पर एक built-in check है. series combination का effective constant छोटा है, तो वो softer और slower oscillate करती है, जबकि parallel combination stiffer और faster. बिलकुल जैसा हम expect करते हैं.
तो discipline साफ़ है: हमेशा पहले effective constant निकालो, फिर period बराबर two pi root m over k-effective लगाओ. दोनों periods को सीधे average करने की कभी कोशिश मत करो, वो meaningless है.

board_events.text: A uniform rod of mass $M$, length $L$, pivots at one end. Use $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/(Mgd)}$.
Since $2L/3 \lt L$, the rod swings faster than a simple pendulum of the same length $L$.
Its mass sits closer to the pivot on average, lowering the effective length to two-thirds of $L$.

segments.text: A J E E Advanced problem that puts the physical pendulum to work. A rigid rod is not a point bob, so we must reach for the moment of inertia.
The picture: a uniform rod of mass M and length L, pivoted at one end, swinging in a vertical plane at small amplitude. The centre of mass sits at the midpoint, a distance L over two from the pivot.
The physical-pendulum formula is period equals two pi root I over M g d, where I is the moment of inertia about the pivot and d is the pivot-to-centre-of-mass distance.
Fill in the two ingredients. For a uniform rod pivoted at one end, the moment of inertia is M L squared over three, and the distance d is L over two.
Substitute both. The M cancels, and inside the root we get L squared over three, divided by g L over two. Simplify and the period is two pi root two L over three g.

Now the equivalent simple-pendulum length, the length of an ideal pendulum that would swing at this same period. It is I over M d, which is M L squared over three divided by M L over two, giving two L over three.

<curious>Here is the punchline. The equivalent length is two-thirds of L, which is less than L. So the rod swings faster than a simple pendulum of the same physical length, by a factor of root three over two.

The reason is physical. The rod's mass is spread out, sitting closer to the pivot on average than a bob at the very end would, which lowers its effective length to two-thirds of L and speeds up the swing.
एक J E E Advanced problem जो physical pendulum को काम पर लगाता है. rigid rod point bob नहीं है, तो हमें moment of inertia की तरफ जाना पड़ेगा.
picture: mass M और length L का uniform rod, एक सिरे पर pivoted, vertical plane में small amplitude पर झूलता. centre of mass midpoint पर बैठता है, pivot से L over two की दूरी पर.
physical-pendulum formula है period बराबर two pi root I over M g d, जहाँ I है pivot के around moment of inertia और d है pivot-to-centre-of-mass distance.
दोनों ingredients भरो. एक सिरे पर pivoted uniform rod के लिए moment of inertia है M L squared over three, और distance d है L over two.
<curious>दोनों substitute करो. M cancel हो जाती है, और root के अंदर मिलता है L squared over three, divided by g L over two. simplify करो तो period है two pi root two L over three g.
अब equivalent simple-pendulum length, यानी उस ideal pendulum की length जो इसी period पर झूले. वो है I over M d, यानी M L squared over three divided by M L over two, यानी two L over three.
यही punchline है. equivalent length है L का दो-तिहाई, जो L से कम है. तो rod उसी physical length के simple pendulum से faster झूलता है, root three over two के factor से.
वजह physical है. rod की mass फैली हुई है, average में सिरे पर रखे bob से pivot के ज़्यादा पास बैठती है, जो इसकी effective length को L के दो-तिहाई तक घटाती है और swing तेज़ कर देती है.

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Five traps around pendulums and springs
The pendulum period is independent of the bob's mass and (small angles) the amplitude; keep both out of $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.
A vertical spring has the same period as a horizontal one; gravity shifts the mean, never the period, and the spring period is independent of $g$.
Parallel springs are stiffer (add the constants); series springs are softer (add the reciprocals). This reverses the resistor rule.
A cut spring piece is stiffer, not weaker: cutting into $n$ equal pieces makes each constant $nk$.
In lifts and cars, replace $g$ by $g_{\text{eff}}$ and get the sign right: up adds, down subtracts, horizontal uses Pythagoras.
When only the static stretch $x_0$ is given, use $T=2\pi\sqrt{x_0/g}$ to sidestep the missing $m$ and $k$.

segments.text: Let us close the pendulum-and-spring subtopic with the five traps that catch students most often, one habit at a time.
First, the pendulum period does not depend on the bob's mass, and for small angles it does not depend on the amplitude either. Keep both firmly out of two pi root L over g.
Second, a vertical spring has the same period as a horizontal one. Gravity only shifts the mean position; it never changes the period, and the spring period is independent of g entirely.

Third, watch series and parallel. Parallel springs are stiffer, so you add the constants; series springs are softer, so you add the reciprocals. This is the reverse of the resistor rule, so do not borrow that intuition.
Fourth, cutting a spring makes each piece stiffer, not weaker. Cut it into n equal pieces and every piece has constant n times k, because a shorter spring stretches less under the same force.
<whisper>Fifth, in any non-inertial frame, a lift or an accelerating car, replace g by g-effective and get the sign right: upward adds, downward subtracts, and horizontal uses Pythagoras.

And a pro-tip for missing data. When a vertical spring's static stretch x-nought is given but the mass and stiffness are not, use period equals two pi root x-nought over g directly, and sidestep the gap.
<chuckle>One line to carry it all: the pendulum feels g-effective, and the spring feels only k. Get those two allegiances right and this whole subtopic falls into place.
चलो pendulum-and-spring subtopic को उन पाँच traps से बंद करें जो students को सबसे ज़्यादा पकड़ते हैं, एक बार में एक आदत.
पहला, pendulum period bob के mass पर depend नहीं करता, और small angles पर amplitude पर भी नहीं. दोनों को two pi root L over g से पक्का बाहर रखो.
दूसरा, vertical spring का period horizontal जैसा ही होता है. gravity सिर्फ़ mean position खिसकाती है; period कभी नहीं बदलती, और spring period पूरी तरह g से independent है.
<whisper>तीसरा, series और parallel देखो. parallel springs stiffer हैं, तो constants जोड़ो; series springs softer हैं, तो reciprocals जोड़ो. ये resistor rule का उल्टा है, तो वो intuition उधार मत लो.
चौथा, spring काटने पर हर piece stiffer होता है, weaker नहीं. n equal pieces में काटो तो हर piece का constant n times k, क्योंकि छोटी spring उसी force पर कम stretch होती है.
पाँचवाँ, किसी भी non-inertial frame में, lift या accelerating car, g की जगह g-effective रखो और sign सही करो: upward जोड़ो, downward घटाओ, और horizontal में Pythagoras.
और missing data के लिए एक pro-tip. जब vertical spring का static stretch x-nought दिया हो पर mass और stiffness नहीं, तो period बराबर two pi root x-nought over g सीधे use करो, और gap को bypass करो.
<chuckle>सब कुछ रखने को एक line: pendulum g-effective महसूस करता है, और spring सिर्फ़ k. उन दो निष्ठाओं को सही रखो और ये पूरा subtopic अपनी जगह बैठ जाता है.

sections.title: Every real oscillation eventually dies

board_events.text: Free, damped, forced: three storylines
Strike a tabla and the note swells then fades; set a jhula swinging and walk away, and within minutes it slows and stops.
Ideal SHM with forever-constant amplitude is a beautiful fiction; reality always leaks energy.

board_events.caption: Free stays constant, damped shrinks, forced settles to a steady swing

board_events.text: Free oscillation: one push, no friction, forever at the natural frequency $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$.
Damped oscillation: a resistive force drains energy, so the amplitude shrinks exponentially while it still oscillates near $\omega_0$.
Forced oscillation: an external periodic force keeps pushing, and after a transient the system marches at the driving frequency.
In the forced steady state, the energy pumped in each cycle exactly replaces what damping removes.

segments.text: The first three subtopics lived in an idealised world where oscillations run forever. Now we face reality, where every oscillation in the world eventually dies.
Strike a tabla and the note swells, then fades. Pluck a sitar string and it sings, then falls silent. Set a child's jhula swinging and walk away, and within a minute or two it slows and stops.
So the forever-constant amplitude of ideal S H M is a beautiful fiction. Reality always leaks energy. Understanding how it leaks, and how we can pump it back in, is the whole of this subtopic.
The picture lines up the three storylines you must keep straight: free stays constant, damped shrinks away, and forced settles to a steady swing.

Free oscillation is the idealised case: give the system one push and leave it alone with no friction, and it oscillates forever at its own natural frequency, omega-nought, the square root of k over m. That is the S H M of the earlier parts.

Damped oscillation is the realistic left-alone case. A resistive force, air drag or internal friction, steadily drains energy, so the amplitude shrinks exponentially, even though the system still oscillates near its natural frequency.

<curious>Forced oscillation is where we refuse to let it die. We apply an external periodic force that keeps pushing. After a brief, confused transient, the system stops using its own frequency and marches instead at the driving frequency.
And in that forced steady state a lovely balance holds: the energy we pump in during each cycle exactly replaces what damping removes, so the amplitude stays constant.
पहले तीन subtopics एक idealised दुनिया में रहते थे जहाँ oscillations हमेशा चलती हैं. अब हम reality का सामना करते हैं, जहाँ दुनिया की हर oscillation आखिरकार मर जाती है.
tabla बजाओ तो note उठती है, फिर fade हो जाती है. sitar की string छेड़ो तो गाती है, फिर चुप हो जाती है. बच्चे का jhula झुलाकर चले जाओ, और एक-दो मिनट में वो धीमा होकर रुक जाता है.
तो ideal S H M का forever-constant amplitude एक सुंदर fiction है. reality हमेशा energy leak करती है. ये कैसे leak होती है, और हम इसे वापस कैसे pump कर सकते हैं, यही पूरा subtopic है.
picture तीन storylines कतार में रख देती है जिन्हें अलग रखना ज़रूरी है: free constant रहती है, damped घटकर मिट जाती है, और forced steady swing पर बैठ जाती है.

<curious>free oscillation idealised case है: system को एक push दो और friction के बिना छोड़ दो, तो वो हमेशा अपनी natural frequency, omega-nought, यानी square root of k over m, पर oscillate करती है. यही पिछले parts की S H M है.

damped oscillation realistic left-alone case है. एक resistive force, air drag या internal friction, लगातार energy निकालती है, तो amplitude exponentially घटती है, जबकि system अब भी अपनी natural frequency के पास oscillate करती है.

forced oscillation वहाँ है जहाँ हम इसे मरने नहीं देते. हम एक external periodic force लगाते हैं जो धकेलती रहती है. एक छोटे, confused transient के बाद, system अपनी frequency छोड़कर driving frequency पर march करती है.
और उस forced steady state में एक प्यारा balance रहता है: हर cycle में हम जो energy pump करते हैं वो exactly उतनी replace करती है जितनी damping निकालती है, तो amplitude constant रहती है.

sections.title: Resonance and the shape of the damping force

board_events.text: A drag that opposes velocity, a push that builds amplitude
The damping force opposes velocity, $F_{\text{damp}}=-bv$: the faster the motion, the harder the medium resists.
Because it always opposes velocity, damping always does negative work, so mechanical energy only ever decreases.

board_events.text: Push a swing at random and it never climbs; push in time with its own rhythm and every push adds energy.
That perfect timing is resonance: when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, the amplitude grows dramatically.
Resonance tunes a radio to one station, and warns soldiers to break step when crossing a bridge.
With zero damping the resonance amplitude would be infinite; real damping keeps it large but finite.

segments.text: Before the formulas, let us build the two central pictures: what the damping force looks like, and what resonance feels like.
The damping force is taken to be proportional to velocity, minus b times v. The faster the body moves, the harder the medium resists it. It is a drag that grows with speed.
And because it always points opposite to the velocity, it always does negative work on the body. So mechanical energy under damping can only ever decrease, never grow.
Now the picture that everyone already knows in their body: pushing a child on a swing.

If you shove at random moments, sometimes you help and sometimes you fight the motion, and the swing never gets very high. But if you time each push to arrive exactly as the swing starts moving away from you, at the swing's own natural rhythm, every push adds energy and the swing climbs higher and higher.
<excited>That perfect timing has a name: resonance. When the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, the amplitude grows dramatically. It is the single most important idea in this subtopic.

And it cuts both ways in the real world. Resonance is how a radio tuner selects one station out of many, an electrical resonance. And it is why soldiers are ordered to break step crossing a bridge, lest their rhythmic marching match the bridge's natural frequency and shake it apart.

One subtlety to hold. If there were literally no damping, the resonance formula would predict an infinite amplitude, which is unphysical. It stays large but finite precisely because every real system carries some damping.
formulas से पहले, दो central pictures बना लेते हैं: damping force कैसी दिखती है, और resonance कैसा महसूस होता है.
damping force velocity के proportional मानी जाती है, minus b times v. body जितनी तेज़ चलती है, medium उतना ज़्यादा resist करता है. ये एक drag है जो speed के साथ बढ़ती है.
और चूँकि ये हमेशा velocity के opposite point करती है, ये हमेशा body पर negative work करती है. तो damping के under mechanical energy सिर्फ़ घट सकती है, कभी बढ़ नहीं.
<excited>अब वो picture जो सबके शरीर को पहले से पता है: बच्चे को swing पर धकेलना.

अगर तुम random पलों पर धक्का दो, कभी help कभी motion से लड़ाई, और swing कभी ज़्यादा ऊँचा नहीं जाता. पर अगर हर push ठीक तब पहुँचे जब swing तुमसे दूर जाना शुरू करे, swing की अपनी natural rhythm पर, तो हर push energy जोड़ता है और swing ऊँचा और ऊँचा चढ़ता है.
उस perfect timing का एक नाम है: resonance. जब driving frequency natural frequency से match करती है, amplitude dramatically बढ़ती है. यही इस subtopic का सबसे ज़रूरी idea है.

और असल दुनिया में ये दोनों तरफ़ काटता है. resonance ही radio tuner को कई में से एक station चुनने देता है, एक electrical resonance. और इसी वजह से soldiers को bridge पार करते वक़्त break step का आदेश मिलता है, कहीं उनकी rhythmic marching bridge की natural frequency से match करके उसे हिला न दे.

एक subtlety पकड़ो. अगर सचमुच कोई damping न हो, तो resonance formula infinite amplitude predict करता, जो unphysical है. ये large पर finite ठीक इसलिए रहती है क्योंकि हर real system में कुछ damping होती है.

sections.title: Formula board: damped motion and its regimes

board_events.text: Decay, shifted frequency, and the three regimes

board_events.latex: A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}, \qquad E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}

board_events.caption: Underdamped oscillates; critical returns fastest; overdamped returns slowly

board_events.text: Energy decays twice as fast as amplitude, because $E\propto A^2$, a direct link back to SHM energy.
Underdamped ($b\lt b_c$) oscillates; critical ($b=b_c$) returns fastest without oscillating; overdamped ($b\gt b_c$) returns slowly.

segments.text: Here is the formula board for a damped oscillator that is left alone. Every line has a clear physical reading.
The displacement is A-nought times e to the minus b t over two m, times cosine of omega-prime t plus phi. Read it as a cosine wrapped inside a shrinking exponential.
The oscillation runs at a shifted frequency, omega-prime, the square root of omega-nought squared minus b over two m, all squared. The natural frequency omega-nought is still root k over m.
The two decay laws are the heart of it. Amplitude falls as e to the minus b t over two m. Energy falls as e to the minus b t over m, twice as fast.

The picture shows the three regimes by how the system returns to equilibrium. Underdamped oscillates as it settles; critical returns fastest with no overshoot; overdamped returns slowly without oscillating.
<whisper>Notice why energy decays twice as fast. Energy goes as amplitude squared, so squaring the amplitude's exponential doubles the exponent. It is a direct callback to the S H M energy subtopic.
The boundary between regimes is critical damping, where b equals two root m k. That is the dividing line.

So the classification is clean. Below critical, the system is underdamped and oscillates. Exactly at critical, it returns fastest without oscillating. Above critical, it is overdamped and returns slowly.
ये रहा एक left-alone damped oscillator का formula board. हर line का एक साफ़ physical reading है.
displacement है A-nought times e to the minus b t over two m, times cosine of omega-prime t plus phi. इसे एक cosine समझो जो एक shrinking exponential के अंदर लिपटी है.
oscillation एक shifted frequency, omega-prime, पर चलती है, यानी square root of omega-nought squared minus b over two m, पूरा squared. natural frequency omega-nought अब भी root k over m है.
<whisper>दो decay laws इसका दिल हैं. amplitude गिरती है e to the minus b t over two m की तरह. energy गिरती है e to the minus b t over m की तरह, दुगुनी तेज़.

picture तीन regimes दिखाती है कि system equilibrium पर कैसे लौटता है. underdamped settle होते हुए oscillate करता है; critical बिना overshoot सबसे तेज़ लौटता है; overdamped बिना oscillate किए धीरे लौटता है.

ध्यान दो energy दुगुनी तेज़ क्यों घटती है. energy amplitude के square पर जाती है, तो amplitude के exponential को square करने पर exponent दुगुना हो जाता है. ये सीधे S H M energy subtopic की याद दिलाता है.
regimes के बीच की सीमा critical damping है, जहाँ b बराबर two root m k. यही बँटवारे की रेखा है.
तो classification साफ़ है. critical से नीचे system underdamped है और oscillate करता है. ठीक critical पर बिना oscillate किए सबसे तेज़ लौटता है. critical से ऊपर overdamped है और धीरे लौटता है.

sections.title: Formula board: forced oscillation and resonance

board_events.text: Driven amplitude, the resonance peak, and quality factor

board_events.caption: Sharper peak for small damping (high Q), broader for large damping

board_events.text: Light damping means $\omega'\approx\omega_0$, so resonance sits essentially at the natural frequency.
A high-$Q$ oscillator rings for about $Q/2\pi$ cycles before its energy falls to $1/e$.

segments.text: Now the forced-oscillation board, built around one master formula for the steady-state amplitude.

Under a driving force F-nought cosine omega t, the steady amplitude is F-nought over m, divided by the square root of two terms: omega squared minus omega-nought squared, all squared, plus b omega over m, squared.

The picture is the resonance curve, and it repays study. For small damping you get a tall, narrow peak, a high quality factor. For large damping, a short, broad peak, a low quality factor. Both peak near omega-nought.

The peak sits at the resonant frequency, omega-r, which for light damping is essentially omega-nought. At that peak the amplitude is about F-nought over b omega-nought, the damping-controlled maximum.

The two limits are worth memorising. As the driving frequency goes to zero, the amplitude tends to F-nought over k, a slow push just statically stretching the spring. Near omega-nought, it rises to F-nought over b omega-nought.
<excited>And the sharpness of the resonance has a name: the quality factor Q, which is m omega-nought over b, and also two pi times the energy stored divided by the energy lost per cycle.
Keep the light-damping simplification in view. When damping is light, the damped frequency omega-prime is nearly omega-nought, so resonance sits essentially at the natural frequency.
And one memorable consequence of Q: a high-quality oscillator rings for about Q over two pi cycles before its energy falls to one over e. High Q means a long, selective ring.
अब forced-oscillation board, जो steady-state amplitude के एक master formula के around बना है.

driving force F-nought cosine omega t के under, steady amplitude है F-nought over m, divided by square root of दो terms: omega squared minus omega-nought squared, पूरा squared, plus b omega over m, squared.

picture resonance curve है, और ये पढ़ने लायक है. small damping के लिए एक tall, narrow peak मिलती है, high quality factor. large damping के लिए short, broad peak, low quality factor. दोनों omega-nought के पास peak करती हैं.
<excited>peak resonant frequency, omega-r, पर बैठती है, जो light damping के लिए essentially omega-nought है. उस peak पर amplitude लगभग F-nought over b omega-nought है, damping-controlled maximum.

दो limits याद रखने लायक हैं. जैसे driving frequency zero की तरफ जाती है, amplitude F-nought over k की तरफ जाती है, एक slow push जो spring को बस statically stretch करता है. omega-nought के पास ये F-nought over b omega-nought तक उठती है.
और resonance की sharpness का एक नाम है: quality factor Q, जो है m omega-nought over b, और two pi times energy stored divided by energy lost per cycle भी.
light-damping simplification नज़र में रखो. जब damping light हो, damped frequency omega-prime लगभग omega-nought है, तो resonance essentially natural frequency पर बैठती है.
और Q का एक यादगार consequence: high-quality oscillator लगभग Q over two pi cycles तक ring करता है इससे पहले कि इसकी energy one over e तक गिरे. high Q मतलब लंबी, selective ring.

sections.title: Framework: the damped oscillator and exponential decay

board_events.text: An oscillation multiplied by a shrinking factor
A mass on a spring in a resistive medium feels drag $-bv$; Newton's law gives the governing equation.
For light damping we expect an oscillation multiplied by a shrinking factor.

board_events.caption: The cosine carries the to-and-fro; the exponential is the shrinking envelope

board_events.text: Damping shrinks amplitude and slightly slows the oscillation, but the shift goes as $b^2$, so it is usually negligible.

segments.text: The first framework builds the damped oscillator from Newton's law and reads the exponential decay straight out of it.
Set up the physics. A mass m on a spring of constant k moves through a medium that exerts a velocity-proportional drag, minus b v. Collect the forces with Newton's second law.
That gives the governing equation: m times x-double-dot, plus b times x-dot, plus k x, equals zero. A spring term, a damping term, and inertia, all balancing.

Now reason about the solution rather than grinding through it. For light damping the system still oscillates, but each swing is a little smaller than the last. So we expect an oscillation multiplied by a shrinking factor.
The picture is exactly that shape. A cosine carries the to-and-fro, and the dashed exponential envelope, plus or minus A-nought e to the minus b t over two m, squeezes it down over time.

Substitute that guess back into the equation and it fixes the frequency at omega-prime, the square root of omega-nought squared minus b over two m squared. The cosine handles the oscillation, the exponential handles the decay.

<curious>Read the physics. Damping does two things: it shrinks the amplitude and it slightly slows the oscillation. But the frequency shift depends on b squared, so for light damping it is negligible; the conspicuous effect is the amplitude decay, not any change of pitch.

Finally the energy. Because mechanical energy is one half k amplitude squared, and the amplitude carries e to the minus b t over two m, the energy carries e to the minus b t over m. Energy falls with half the time-constant of the amplitude, a favourite exam catch.
पहला framework damped oscillator को Newton के law से बनाता है और exponential decay सीधे उसमें से पढ़ता है.
physics set करो. constant k की spring पर mass m एक medium में चलती है जो velocity-proportional drag, minus b v, लगाता है. Newton के second law से forces इकट्ठा करो.
इससे governing equation मिलती है: m times x-double-dot, plus b times x-dot, plus k x, बराबर zero. एक spring term, एक damping term, और inertia, सब balance करते.

अब solution को grind करने के बजाय उस पर reason करो. light damping के लिए system अब भी oscillate करता है, पर हर swing पिछले से थोड़ी छोटी. तो हम expect करते हैं एक oscillation जो एक shrinking factor से multiply हो.
<curious>picture बिलकुल वही shape है. एक cosine to-and-fro रखती है, और dashed exponential envelope, plus या minus A-nought e to the minus b t over two m, इसे समय के साथ दबा देती है.
उस guess को equation में वापस रखो तो frequency omega-prime पर fix हो जाती है, square root of omega-nought squared minus b over two m squared. cosine oscillation सँभालती है, exponential decay.

physics पढ़ो. damping दो काम करती है: amplitude घटाती है और oscillation थोड़ा slow करती है. पर frequency shift b squared पर depend करता है, तो light damping के लिए negligible है; दिखने वाला effect amplitude decay है, कोई pitch बदलाव नहीं.

आखिर में energy. चूँकि mechanical energy है one half k amplitude squared, और amplitude e to the minus b t over two m रखती है, energy e to the minus b t over m रखती है. energy amplitude के आधे time-constant से गिरती है, एक favourite exam catch.

sections.title: Framework: forced oscillation, steady state, and resonance

board_events.text: Reading the whole resonance story off one denominator
After the transient dies, the only sustainable rhythm is the driver's, so $x=A\cos(\omega t-\delta)$ at the driving frequency.

board_events.caption: Low frequency gives F0 over k; the peak sits at resonance; damping caps it

board_events.text: The first term $(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)^2$ vanishes when the drive matches $\omega_0$, making the amplitude shoot up.
Damping alone keeps the denominator off zero, capping the resonant amplitude at about $F_0/(b\omega_0)$.
Set $\omega\to 0$ and the amplitude collapses to $F_0/k$: a slow push just statically stretches the spring.

segments.text: The second framework adds an external drive and shows that the entire resonance story is encoded in a single denominator.
Add a periodic force to the equation: m x-double-dot, plus b x-dot, plus k x, equals F-nought cosine omega t. The right-hand side is the new driver.

Reason about the steady state. After the transient dies away, the only rhythm the system can sustain is the one the driver imposes. So the steady motion is A cosine of omega t minus delta, oscillating at the driving frequency but lagging the force by a phase delta.

Substituting and balancing the spring, damping, and inertial terms yields the amplitude: F-nought over m, divided by the square root of omega squared minus omega-nought squared, squared, plus b omega over m, squared.
Now read the picture, which is just this amplitude plotted against driving frequency. Look at the denominator to understand every feature of the curve.
The first term, omega squared minus omega-nought squared, all squared, vanishes exactly when the drive matches the natural frequency. That is what makes the amplitude shoot up at resonance.

<excited>But it never quite reaches infinity. The second term, b omega over m squared, is the only thing keeping the denominator off zero, so damping alone caps the resonant amplitude at about F-nought over b omega-nought.

And the other end confirms the reading. Set the driving frequency to zero and the amplitude collapses to F-nought over k. A slow push simply stretches the spring statically. One denominator, and the whole resonance story falls out.
दूसरा framework एक external drive जोड़ता है और दिखाता है कि पूरी resonance कहानी एक ही denominator में encode है.
equation में एक periodic force जोड़ो: m x-double-dot, plus b x-dot, plus k x, बराबर F-nought cosine omega t. right-hand side नया driver है.

steady state पर reason करो. transient मिटने के बाद, system सिर्फ़ वही rhythm sustain कर सकती है जो driver थोपता है. तो steady motion है A cosine of omega t minus delta, driving frequency पर oscillate करती पर force से एक phase delta पीछे.

substitute करके spring, damping, और inertial terms balance करने पर amplitude मिलती है: F-nought over m, divided by square root of omega squared minus omega-nought squared, squared, plus b omega over m, squared.
<excited>अब picture पढ़ो, जो बस यही amplitude driving frequency के against plotted है. curve के हर feature को समझने के लिए denominator देखो.
पहला term, omega squared minus omega-nought squared, पूरा squared, ठीक तब vanish होता है जब drive natural frequency से match करे. यही amplitude को resonance पर उछाल देता है.
पर ये कभी infinity तक नहीं पहुँचता. दूसरा term, b omega over m squared, ही denominator को zero से बचाता है, तो damping अकेली resonant amplitude को लगभग F-nought over b omega-nought पर cap करती है.

और दूसरा सिरा reading confirm करता है. driving frequency zero रखो तो amplitude F-nought over k पर गिर जाती है. एक slow push बस spring को statically stretch करता है. एक denominator, और पूरी resonance कहानी निकल आती है.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): time for the amplitude to halve

board_events.text: Exponential decay and equal halving times
Given: mass 0.2 kg, damping constant $b=0.04$ kg/s. Find the time for the amplitude to fall to half. Take $\ln 2 = 0.693$.
So the amplitude halves in about 6.9 s.
It halves again in the next 6.9 s: equal times for equal fractional drops, the signature of exponential decay.
You rarely need $b$ by itself; exploit the equal-interval property of exponentials.
Every fixed-ratio drop takes the same time, whatever the ratio.

segments.text: A clean C B S E numerical on damping, and it hides a beautiful property of exponentials that saves time on harder problems.

The data: the mass is zero point two kilograms and the damping constant b is zero point zero four kilograms per second. Find the time for the amplitude to drop to half its initial value, taking the natural log of two as zero point six nine three.
The amplitude obeys A-nought times e to the minus b t over two m. Set that equal to half of A-nought. The A-noughts cancel, and taking logs gives b t over two m equals the natural log of two.

Solve for the time. It is two m over b, times the log of two: two times zero point two over zero point zero four, which is ten, times zero point six nine three. That comes to six point nine three seconds.
So the amplitude halves in about six point nine seconds. A single clean number.

<chuckle>Now the beautiful part. It halves again in the next six point nine seconds, and again in the six point nine after that. Equal times for equal fractional drops is the signature of exponential decay.
That property means you rarely need to find b on its own. Once you know one halving time, you know them all, because each one is identical.

And it generalises past halving. Every fixed-ratio drop, to a third, to a tenth, whatever, takes the same fixed time. Exploit that equal-interval rhythm and many damping problems become almost instant.
damping पर एक साफ़ C B S E numerical, और ये exponentials की एक सुंदर property छुपाता है जो मुश्किल problems पर time बचाती है.
data: mass zero point two kilograms और damping constant b zero point zero four kilograms per second. amplitude के आधे होने का time निकालो, natural log of two को zero point six nine three लेते हुए.
amplitude मानती है A-nought times e to the minus b t over two m. इसे A-nought के आधे के बराबर रखो. A-noughts cancel, और logs लेने पर b t over two m बराबर natural log of two.
time के लिए solve करो. ये है two m over b, times log of two: two times zero point two over zero point zero four, यानी ten, times zero point six nine three. जो बनता है six point nine three seconds.
<chuckle>तो amplitude लगभग six point nine seconds में आधी होती है. एक साफ़ number.
अब सुंदर हिस्सा. ये अगले six point nine seconds में फिर आधी होती है, और उसके बाद के six point nine में फिर. equal fractional drops के लिए equal times exponential decay की पहचान है.
उस property का मतलब है तुम्हें b अकेले निकालने की कम ही ज़रूरत पड़ती है. एक halving time पता चलते ही सब पता, क्योंकि हर एक identical है.
और ये halving से आगे भी चलता है. हर fixed-ratio drop, एक-तिहाई तक, एक-दसवें तक, जो भी, वही fixed time लेता है. उस equal-interval rhythm को use करो और बहुत damping problems लगभग instant हो जाते हैं.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): the resonant driving frequency

board_events.text: Maximum amplitude sits at the natural frequency
A spring-mass system has natural frequency 5 Hz. A small periodic force drives it. At roughly what frequency is the amplitude largest, and what is it called?
The trap: do not grind out $\omega_r=\sqrt{\omega_0^2 - b^2/2m^2}$, and never guess twice or half the natural frequency.
For the light damping implied by a small force, the correction term is negligible.
Maximum amplitude always sits at (or near) the natural frequency, never at a multiple of it.
The phenomenon is resonance.
Answer: about 5 Hz, and the phenomenon is resonance.

segments.text: A short, sharp N E E T conceptual question that rewards knowing where resonance lives rather than reaching for a formula.

A spring-mass system has a natural frequency of five hertz. A small periodic driving force is applied. At approximately what driving frequency is the amplitude largest, and what is the phenomenon called?

Here is the trap. A student may try to compute the exact resonant frequency, the square root of omega-nought squared minus b squared over two m squared, and get bogged down. Worse, some guess that maximum amplitude sits at twice or half the natural frequency.

But look at the phrase small periodic force. Small force implies light damping, so the correction term is negligible, and the amplitude peaks essentially at the natural frequency. The driving frequency is about five hertz.
That is the whole calculation, because the light-damping approximation does all the work for you.

<whisper>Lock in the principle. Maximum amplitude always sits at, or very near, the natural frequency, and never at a multiple of it. Twice and half are pure distractors borrowed from the waves chapter.
And the name for this is resonance, the matching of the drive to the system's own rhythm.
So the answer is compact: the amplitude is largest at about five hertz, and the phenomenon is resonance. No grinding required.
एक छोटा, तीखा N E E T conceptual सवाल जो resonance कहाँ रहता है ये जानने को इनाम देता है, formula की तरफ जाने को नहीं.
एक spring-mass system की natural frequency five hertz है. एक small periodic driving force लगाई जाती है. लगभग किस driving frequency पर amplitude सबसे बड़ी है, और इस phenomenon को क्या कहते हैं?

<whisper>यही रहा trap. student exact resonant frequency, square root of omega-nought squared minus b squared over two m squared, निकालने की कोशिश कर सकता है और उलझ जाता है. और बुरा, कुछ guess करते हैं कि maximum amplitude natural frequency की दुगुनी या आधी पर है.

पर phrase small periodic force देखो. small force मतलब light damping, तो correction term negligible है, और amplitude essentially natural frequency पर peak करती है. driving frequency लगभग five hertz है.
यही पूरा calculation है, क्योंकि light-damping approximation सारा काम तुम्हारे लिए कर देती है.
principle पक्का करो. maximum amplitude हमेशा natural frequency पर, या उसके बहुत पास, बैठती है, और कभी उसके multiple पर नहीं. दुगुनी और आधी pure distractors हैं, waves chapter से उधार.
और इसका नाम है resonance, drive का system की अपनी rhythm से match होना.
तो answer compact है: amplitude लगभग five hertz पर सबसे बड़ी है, और phenomenon है resonance. कोई grinding नहीं चाहिए.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): frequencies, decay time, and energy left

board_events.text: Light damping barely moves the frequency
Given: mass 0.5 kg, spring constant 50 N/m, damping constant 0.1 kg/s. Find the natural and damped frequencies, the $1/e$ amplitude time, and the energy fraction left.
The frequency is essentially unchanged, confirming the damping is light.
Cross-check: at $A=A_0/e$, $E\propto A^2 = E_0/e^2 = 0.135\,E_0$, about 13.5% remaining.

segments.text: A three-part J E E Main numerical that puts the damped formulas to work and demonstrates just how gently light damping touches the frequency.

The data: mass zero point five kilograms, spring constant fifty newtons per metre, damping constant zero point one kilograms per second. Find the natural and damped angular frequencies, the time for the amplitude to fall to one over e, and the fraction of energy remaining then.
Start with the natural frequency. Omega-nought is root k over m, root fifty over zero point five, which is root one hundred, exactly ten radians per second.

Now the damped frequency. b over two m is zero point one over one, which is zero point one, so omega-prime is root of one hundred minus zero point zero one, root ninety-nine point nine nine, about ten point zero radians per second.
See the point. The damped frequency is essentially identical to the natural one. That tiny difference confirms the damping here is light.
For the one-over-e amplitude time, set b t over two m equal to one, so the time is two m over b, which is two times zero point five over zero point one, ten seconds.

<curious>For the energy, use energy decays as e to the minus b t over m. At ten seconds, b t over m is zero point one times ten over zero point five, which is two. So the energy is E-nought times e to the minus two, about zero point one three five of E-nought.

And the cross-check ties it together. When the amplitude is A-nought over e, the energy, going as amplitude squared, is E-nought over e squared, which is zero point one three five of E-nought. About thirteen and a half percent of the energy remains. Both routes agree.
एक तीन-हिस्से वाला J E E Main numerical जो damped formulas को काम पर लगाता है और दिखाता है कि light damping frequency को कितनी हल्की छूती है.

data: mass zero point five kilograms, spring constant fifty newtons per metre, damping constant zero point one kilograms per second. natural और damped angular frequencies, amplitude के one over e तक गिरने का time, और तब बची energy का fraction निकालो.
natural frequency से शुरू करो. omega-nought है root k over m, root fifty over zero point five, यानी root one hundred, exactly ten radians per second.

अब damped frequency. b over two m है zero point one over one, यानी zero point one, तो omega-prime है root of one hundred minus zero point zero one, root ninety-nine point nine nine, लगभग ten point zero radians per second.
<curious>बात समझो. damped frequency essentially natural जितनी ही है. वो छोटा फ़र्क़ confirm करता है कि यहाँ damping light है.
one-over-e amplitude time के लिए b t over two m को one के बराबर रखो, तो time है two m over b, यानी two times zero point five over zero point one, ten seconds.

energy के लिए use करो energy घटती है e to the minus b t over m की तरह. ten seconds पर b t over m है zero point one times ten over zero point five, यानी two. तो energy है E-nought times e to the minus two, लगभग zero point one three five of E-nought.

और cross-check सब जोड़ देता है. जब amplitude A-nought over e हो, energy, amplitude squared पर जाती हुई, है E-nought over e squared, यानी zero point one three five of E-nought. लगभग thirteen and a half percent energy बची. दोनों routes agree करते हैं.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): the meaning of the quality factor

board_events.text: How many cycles does a high-Q oscillator ring?
Given: natural angular frequency $\omega_0=200$ rad/s and quality factor $Q=100$. Find $b/m$ and the cycles before the energy falls to $1/e$.

board_events.caption: The oscillator rings for about Q over two pi cycles before its energy falls to one over e

board_events.text: So the system completes about 16 oscillations, and in general $N = Q/2\pi$.
A high-$Q$ oscillator rings for many cycles, which is why a high-$Q$ tuning circuit gives a sharp, selective resonance.

segments.text: A J E E Advanced problem that turns the quality factor from a definition into a picture: how many times does a good oscillator ring before its energy fades?

The data: the natural angular frequency is two hundred radians per second, and the quality factor Q is one hundred. Find the ratio b over m, then estimate the number of complete oscillations before the energy falls to one over e.
Start from the definition Q equals m omega-nought over b. Rearranging, b over m is omega-nought over Q, which is two hundred over one hundred, so b over m is two per second.

Now the time for the energy to fall to one over e. Set E-nought times e to the minus b over m times t equal to E-nought over e, so b over m times t is one, and the time is m over b, which is zero point five seconds.
The picture shows what that means: a slowly-decaying ring, with the moment its energy reaches one over e marked well to the right, after many full cycles.

<excited>Now count the cycles. The period is two pi over omega-nought, two pi over two hundred, about zero point zero three one four seconds. The number of oscillations is the time over the period, which tidies beautifully to m omega-nought over two pi b, that is Q over two pi, about fifteen point nine.
So the system completes about sixteen oscillations, and in general the number of rings is Q over two pi. That is a clean, memorable link between the quality factor and the count of visible swings.

And this is the deep meaning of Q. A high-quality oscillator rings for many cycles before its energy decays, which is exactly why a high-Q tuning circuit gives a sharp, selective resonance, the very thing that lets a radio pick one station cleanly.
एक J E E Advanced problem जो quality factor को definition से picture में बदल देता है: एक अच्छा oscillator अपनी energy मिटने से पहले कितनी बार ring करता है?

data: natural angular frequency two hundred radians per second, और quality factor Q one hundred. ratio b over m निकालो, फिर energy के one over e तक गिरने से पहले complete oscillations की संख्या estimate करो.
definition Q बराबर m omega-nought over b से शुरू करो. rearrange करो तो b over m है omega-nought over Q, यानी two hundred over one hundred, तो b over m है two per second.

अब energy के one over e तक गिरने का time. E-nought times e to the minus b over m times t को E-nought over e के बराबर रखो, तो b over m times t है one, और time है m over b, यानी zero point five seconds.
<excited>picture दिखाती है इसका मतलब क्या: एक धीरे-decay होती ring, जिसमें energy के one over e तक पहुँचने का पल दाईं तरफ़ दूर marked है, कई पूरे cycles के बाद.

अब cycles गिनो. period है two pi over omega-nought, two pi over two hundred, लगभग zero point zero three one four seconds. oscillations की संख्या है time over period, जो सुंदर तरह से m omega-nought over two pi b तक साफ़ होती है, यानी Q over two pi, लगभग fifteen point nine.
तो system लगभग sixteen oscillations पूरे करता है, और general में rings की संख्या है Q over two pi. ये quality factor और दिखने वाले swings की गिनती के बीच एक साफ़, यादगार link है.

और यही Q का गहरा मतलब है. high-quality oscillator अपनी energy मिटने से पहले कई cycles ring करता है, ठीक इसीलिए high-Q tuning circuit एक sharp, selective resonance देता है, वही चीज़ जो radio को एक station साफ़ चुनने देती है.

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Five traps in damping and resonance
Light damping barely slows the frequency; the visible effect is shrinking amplitude, and the shift goes as $b^2$.
In the forced steady state the system vibrates at the driving frequency, never at its own natural frequency; that belongs to the transient.
Resonance amplitude is finite, not infinite, because real systems always have some damping.
Energy decays twice as fast as amplitude: $A\propto e^{-bt/2m}$ but $E\propto e^{-bt/m}$, because $E\propto A^2$.
Critical damping gives the fastest no-oscillation return; overdamping is also non-oscillatory but slower; underdamping still oscillates.
For amplitude-fraction problems, exploit the equal-interval property: each fixed-ratio drop takes the same time.

board_events.latex: \textbf{Sharpness:}\ Q = \dfrac{2\pi}{\text{fractional energy lost per cycle}},\quad N \approx \dfrac{Q}{2\pi}

segments.text: Let us close damped and forced oscillations with the five traps that catch students, most of them born from picturing damping wrongly.

First, do not believe damping noticeably slows the frequency. For light damping the damped frequency is nearly the natural one; the visible effect is the shrinking amplitude, and the frequency shift goes only as b squared, usually negligible.

Second, do not confuse transient with steady state. In the steady state of a forced oscillation the system vibrates at the driving frequency, never at its own natural frequency. Its natural-frequency motion belongs only to the brief transient.
Third, resonance amplitude is finite, not infinite. It is capped because every real system carries some damping; only the idealised zero-damping formula blows up.
Fourth, remember that energy decays twice as fast as amplitude. Amplitude goes as e to the minus b t over two m, but energy goes as e to the minus b t over m, because energy is amplitude squared.

<whisper>Fifth, keep the three regimes straight. Critical damping gives the fastest return with no oscillation; overdamping is also non-oscillatory but slower; underdamping still oscillates as it settles.
And a pro-tip for amplitude-fraction problems: exploit the equal-interval property. Each fixed-ratio drop takes the same time, so you rarely need to solve for b at all.

<chuckle>Finally, two sharpness shortcuts worth memorising: Q is two pi divided by the fractional energy lost per cycle, and the oscillator rings for about Q over two pi cycles before its energy falls to one over e.
चलो damped and forced oscillations को उन पाँच traps से बंद करें जो students को पकड़ते हैं, ज़्यादातर damping को गलत picture करने से पैदा.

पहला, ये मत मानो कि damping frequency को ध्यान देने लायक slow करती है. light damping के लिए damped frequency लगभग natural जितनी है; दिखने वाला effect shrinking amplitude है, और frequency shift सिर्फ़ b squared पर जाता है, आमतौर पर negligible.

दूसरा, transient और steady state को मत उलझाओ. forced oscillation के steady state में system driving frequency पर vibrate करती है, कभी अपनी natural frequency पर नहीं. उसकी natural-frequency motion सिर्फ़ छोटे transient की है.
<whisper>तीसरा, resonance amplitude finite है, infinite नहीं. ये cap होती है क्योंकि हर real system में कुछ damping है; सिर्फ़ idealised zero-damping formula उड़ जाता है.
चौथा, याद रखो energy amplitude से दुगुनी तेज़ घटती है. amplitude e to the minus b t over two m पर जाती है, पर energy e to the minus b t over m पर, क्योंकि energy amplitude squared है.
पाँचवाँ, तीन regimes साफ़ रखो. critical damping बिना oscillation सबसे तेज़ return देता है; overdamping भी non-oscillatory पर slower; underdamping settle होते हुए भी oscillate करता है.
और amplitude-fraction problems के लिए एक pro-tip: equal-interval property use करो. हर fixed-ratio drop वही time लेता है, तो तुम्हें b निकालने की कम ही ज़रूरत पड़ती है.

<chuckle>आखिर में, दो sharpness shortcuts याद रखने लायक: Q है two pi divided by per cycle खोई fractional energy, और oscillator लगभग Q over two pi cycles ring करता है इससे पहले कि इसकी energy one over e तक गिरे.

sections.subtopic: Reference Circle, Superposition and More SHM Systems
sections.title: The reference circle: SHM is a shadow

board_events.text: Uniform circular motion, seen edge-on
A bead circulates steadily on a turntable of radius $A$; its shadow on a wall runs back and forth in a line, executing exactly SHM.

board_events.caption: The projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter is SHM

board_events.text: This is an identity, not an analogy: the amplitude is the radius, $\omega$ the circulation rate, and the phase the angle swept.
The bead moves at constant speed, but its shadow does not: still at the turning points, sprinting through the centre.
A phasor is just this rotating radius, which is why we can add SHMs like vectors.
The rigorous test for SHM is the differential equation itself.

segments.text: This final subtopic hands you three tools that turn S H M from algebra into deep understanding, and let you tackle any oscillator an examiner invents. The first is the reference circle.

Imagine a bead glued to the rim of a turntable spinning at a steady angular speed omega, with radius A. Shine a light from the side and watch the bead's shadow on the wall. As the bead goes round and round, its shadow runs back and forth in a straight line, and that shadow is executing exactly simple harmonic motion.
The picture makes it vivid: the circling bead above, its shadow sliding along the diameter below.

<curious>And this is not a loose analogy; it is a mathematical identity. The three S H M constants suddenly have a picture: the amplitude is the radius of the circle, omega is how fast the bead circulates, and the phase is literally the angle the radius has swept.

Notice the twist. The bead moves at constant speed, but its shadow does not. When the bead is at the top or bottom, the shadow is momentarily still, at a turning point; when the bead crosses the horizontal, the shadow is sprinting through the centre. Constant circular speed, varying shadow speed, in one image.
That rotating radius has a name: a phasor. It is exactly why we can add simple harmonic motions like vectors, which we will use in a moment.
Now the second tool, the rigorous definition. Forget recognising systems by their looks; the real test is the differential equation.
A motion is simple harmonic if and only if its acceleration equals minus omega squared times its displacement. Find that line for any system and it is S H M, with the period falling straight out.
ये आखिरी subtopic तुम्हें तीन tools देता है जो S H M को algebra से गहरी समझ में बदल देते हैं, और किसी भी oscillator से निपटने देते हैं जो examiner बनाए. पहला है reference circle.

सोचो एक bead एक turntable के rim पर चिपका है जो steady angular speed omega पर घूम रहा है, radius A के साथ. side से light डालो और wall पर bead की shadow देखो. जैसे bead घूमता जाता है, इसकी shadow एक सीधी line में आगे पीछे दौड़ती है, और वो shadow exactly simple harmonic motion कर रही है.
picture इसे जीवंत करती है: ऊपर घूमता bead, नीचे diameter पर सरकती इसकी shadow.

<curious>और ये कोई ढीली analogy नहीं है; ये एक mathematical identity है. तीनों S H M constants को अचानक एक picture मिल जाती है: amplitude है circle का radius, omega है bead कितनी तेज़ circulate करता है, और phase है वो angle जो radius ने sweep किया.

twist देखो. bead constant speed पर चलता है, पर इसकी shadow नहीं. जब bead top या bottom पर हो, shadow पल भर के लिए still होती है, एक turning point पर; जब bead horizontal cross करे, shadow centre से गुज़रती हुई दौड़ती है. constant circular speed, बदलती shadow speed, एक ही image में.
उस rotating radius का एक नाम है: phasor. यही वजह है कि हम simple harmonic motions को vectors की तरह जोड़ सकते हैं, जो अभी use करेंगे.
अब दूसरा tool, rigorous definition. systems को उनकी शक्ल से पहचानना भूल जाओ; असली test differential equation है.
कोई motion simple harmonic है if and only if इसका acceleration बराबर हो minus omega squared times इसका displacement. किसी भी system के लिए वो line ढूँढो और वो S H M है, period सीधे निकलता हुआ.

To prove a strange system is SHM, displace it a little, find its restoring force or energy, and show $\ddot{x}=-(\text{positive constant})\,x$.
That constant is $\omega^2$, and the period drops out as $T=2\pi/\omega$: one method for every system.

board_events.text: Two collinear SHMs add like phasors and give another SHM of the same frequency.
Two perpendicular SHMs trace a path: a line, an ellipse, a circle, or a looping Lissajous figure.
The reference-circle equivalence is exact only for uniform circular motion; the SHM test certifies only small displacements.
Collinear superposition gives a single clean SHM only when the two share the same frequency; different frequencies give beats.

segments.text: The second and third tools live here: a universal test that certifies any oscillator, and the superposition of two motions at once.

Here is the universal recipe. To prove that some strange new system, a wobbling test tube, a sloshing liquid, a body falling through the Earth, is simple harmonic, you do not need to recognise it. Displace it a little, find its restoring force or write its energy, and show the acceleration comes out as minus a positive constant, times the displacement.
That constant is omega squared, and the period drops out immediately as two pi over omega. One method, every system, no memorised special cases.
Now superposition, in the picture. Real objects often feel two S H Ms at once, and how they combine depends on their directions.
If the two act along the same line, they add like phasors, like vectors, and the result is another simple harmonic motion of the same frequency.

If they act at right angles, the particle traces a two-dimensional path: a straight line, an ellipse, a circle, or, for unequal frequencies, the beautiful looping Lissajous figures you see on an oscilloscope.

<curious>Two cautions on scope. The reference-circle equivalence is exact only for genuinely uniform circular motion, and the acceleration test certifies simple harmonic motion only for small displacements, where the restoring effect stays linear.

And one more: collinear superposition gives a single clean S H M only when the two components share the same frequency. Two different frequencies do not add to an S H M; they give beats, which is a different story.
दूसरा और तीसरा tool यहाँ रहते हैं: एक universal test जो किसी भी oscillator को certify करता है, और एक साथ दो motions का superposition.

यही रही universal recipe. किसी नए अजीब system को, एक हिलता test tube, एक sloshing liquid, Earth में से गिरता body, simple harmonic साबित करने के लिए तुम्हें उसे पहचानने की ज़रूरत नहीं. उसे थोड़ा displace करो, restoring force ढूँढो या energy लिखो, और दिखाओ कि acceleration निकलता है minus एक positive constant, times displacement.
वो constant है omega squared, और period तुरंत two pi over omega निकल आता है. एक method, हर system, कोई memorised special case नहीं.
अब superposition, picture में. real objects अक्सर एक साथ दो S H Ms महसूस करते हैं, और वो कैसे combine होते हैं ये उनकी directions पर depend करता है.
अगर दोनों एक ही line के साथ हों, वो phasors की तरह, vectors की तरह, जुड़ते हैं, और result उसी frequency का एक और simple harmonic motion होता है.

<curious>अगर वो right angles पर हों, particle एक two-dimensional path बनाती है: एक सीधी line, एक ellipse, एक circle, या unequal frequencies के लिए वो सुंदर looping Lissajous figures जो oscilloscope पर दिखती हैं.

scope पर दो cautions. reference-circle equivalence exact सिर्फ़ genuinely uniform circular motion के लिए है, और acceleration test simple harmonic motion सिर्फ़ small displacements के लिए certify करता है, जहाँ restoring effect linear रहता है.

और एक और: collinear superposition एक single clean S H M सिर्फ़ तब देता है जब दोनों components same frequency share करें. दो अलग frequencies S H M में नहीं जुड़तीं; वो beats देती हैं, जो एक अलग कहानी है.

board_events.text: Unequal frequencies give Lissajous figures; the frequency ratio sets the number of loops.

segments.text: The formula board for this subtopic, in two panels. First the projections and the superposition algebra.

From the reference circle, the projection is x equals A cosine of omega t plus phi. Differentiating gives velocity, minus A omega sine, and acceleration, minus A omega squared cosine, which is again minus omega squared x.
The defining equation, x-double-dot plus omega squared x equals zero, is also the recipe: omega is the square root of the restoring constant over the inertia, whatever those are for your system.

For two collinear S H Ms, the resultant amplitude is the square root of A-one squared plus A-two squared plus twice A-one A-two cosine delta, and the resultant phase has tangent A-two sine delta, over A-one plus A-two cosine delta. It is just the law of cosines for phasors.

The three special cases are worth reflexes. In phase, delta zero, the amplitudes simply add. Anti-phase, delta pi, they subtract in magnitude. In quadrature, delta pi over two, you get the root of the sum of squares.

For perpendicular S H Ms of equal frequency, the picture shows the whole family: in phase gives a line, anti-phase the opposite line, quadrature an ellipse, and equal amplitudes in quadrature a circle.
<whisper>Writing the quadrature case out, x squared over A squared plus y squared over B squared equals one, an ellipse, which becomes a circle when the two amplitudes are equal.
And when the two frequencies are unequal, you no longer get a simple closed curve but a Lissajous figure, whose number of loops is set by the frequency ratio.
इस subtopic का formula board, दो panels में. पहले projections और superposition algebra.

reference circle से projection है x बराबर A cosine of omega t plus phi. differentiate करने पर velocity, minus A omega sine, और acceleration, minus A omega squared cosine, जो फिर minus omega squared x है.
defining equation, x-double-dot plus omega squared x बराबर zero, recipe भी है: omega है square root of restoring constant over inertia, जो भी तुम्हारे system के लिए हों.

दो collinear S H Ms के लिए resultant amplitude है square root of A-one squared plus A-two squared plus twice A-one A-two cosine delta, और resultant phase का tangent है A-two sine delta, over A-one plus A-two cosine delta. ये बस phasors के लिए law of cosines है.

<whisper>तीन special cases reflex बनने लायक हैं. in phase, delta zero, amplitudes बस जुड़ जाती हैं. anti-phase, delta pi, magnitude में घट जाती हैं. quadrature, delta pi over two, sum of squares का root मिलता है.
perpendicular equal-frequency S H Ms के लिए picture पूरा परिवार दिखाती है: in phase एक line देता है, anti-phase उल्टी line, quadrature एक ellipse, और equal amplitudes quadrature में एक circle.
quadrature case लिखो, x squared over A squared plus y squared over B squared बराबर one, एक ellipse, जो circle बन जाती है जब दोनों amplitudes बराबर हों.
और जब दोनों frequencies unequal हों, तुम्हें simple closed curve नहीं बल्कि एक Lissajous figure मिलती है, जिसके loops की संख्या frequency ratio से तय होती है.

segments.text: The second panel collects the standard systems and the pendulum fine points that examiners love.
The picture lines up three systems that look completely different but share one skeleton: a liquid in a U-tube, a floating body, and a body dropped through a tunnel in the Earth.
Their periods: the U-tube is two pi root L over two g, where L is the total column length; the floating body is two pi root h over g, where h is the submerged depth.
The Earth tunnel, and a ball in a smooth bowl, both give two pi root R over g, which works out to about eighty-four point six minutes, a famous number.

Two pendulum fine points. A temperature change shifts the period fractionally by half alpha delta theta, and a rise lengthens the rod so the clock runs slow. And at larger amplitude the period grows by a factor one plus theta-nought squared over sixteen.
For averages over a cycle, the mean speed is four A over the period, equivalently two A omega over pi, and the root-mean-square speed is A omega over root two.
<curious>But the deepest thing to carry is not any single formula, it is the family resemblance.

Keep the period-twins on a sticky note: root L over g, root h over g, root R over g. Pendulum, float, planet. Same skeleton, different length, and once you see it, half these problems solve themselves.
दूसरा panel standard systems और pendulum fine points इकट्ठा करता है जो examiners को पसंद हैं.
picture तीन systems कतार में रखती है जो बिलकुल अलग दिखते हैं पर एक skeleton share करते हैं: U-tube में liquid, एक floating body, और Earth में tunnel से गिरता body.
इनके periods: U-tube है two pi root L over two g, जहाँ L total column length है; floating body है two pi root h over g, जहाँ h submerged depth है.
Earth tunnel, और smooth bowl में ball, दोनों देते हैं two pi root R over g, जो निकलता है लगभग eighty-four point six minutes, एक famous number.

दो pendulum fine points. temperature change period को fractionally half alpha delta theta से shift करता है, और rise rod को लंबा करती है तो clock slow चलता है. और बड़े amplitude पर period one plus theta-nought squared over sixteen के factor से बढ़ता है.
<curious>cycle पर averages के लिए, mean speed है four A over period, यानी two A omega over pi, और root-mean-square speed है A omega over root two.
पर सबसे गहरी बात कोई single formula नहीं, वो है family resemblance.
period-twins sticky note पर रखो: root L over g, root h over g, root R over g. pendulum, float, planet. वही skeleton, अलग length, और एक बार दिख जाए तो आधे ये problems खुद हल हो जाते हैं.
